It's Time to Stop Tracking Screen Time — And Start Living In the Digital Age

📅 02 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3073 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Way too much falls on parents when it comes to screen time.
  • Sources indicate that the war for our kids' attention is being waged, and we’re losing.
  • According to recent reports, I’ve signed the Wait Until 8th pledge, I’m working on ways for the kids to be more independent (both commute to school themselves!), and we talk about screen time an annoying amount.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Way too much falls on parents when it comes to screen time. There’s another way.

Sources indicate that the war for our kids' attention is being waged, and we’re losing. That’s my cynical summary of so many experts who study such things. When it comes to screen science, I’ve attended the lectures, seen the documentaries, read the books, gone to parent meetups, and flipped through the studies. I’ve been through it personally with my high schooler — hooked, caught in dangerous situations, experiencing mental health crises thanks to the online world. My third-grader is phone-free and blissfully unaware (well, he loves Tears of the Kingdom, but that seems downright educational these days), but I still work so hard to get ahead of it.

According to recent reports, I’ve signed the Wait Until 8th pledge, I’m working on ways for the kids to be more independent (both commute to school themselves!), and we talk about screen time an annoying amount. Hell, I’ve helped to start and run a PTA committee whose purpose is to look critically at screen time and help foster independence in kids. There’s a lot of movement. And yet, it feels like parents are American revolutionaries in 1773. We’re dumping tea into the harbor and an impossibly well-funded army is coming to get us.

It has been revealed that this past week I took the fight overseas. I had the pleasure of talking with Kaitlyn Regehr, Ph.D., a researcher and professor of digital humanities at University College London and author of Smartphone Nation, out now. The tagline of the book is spot on: “Building Digital Boundaries When Offline Isn't an Option.” It’s a go-to book that’s informative, but not overly complex, exhaustive, but surprisingly short and to the point, and lacking in the shame that so many screen time books put on parents. I can't recommend it enough.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

According to recent reports, I'd love to start with the idea of digital pyramids, if that's OK. Like the food pyramid, it can be a really helpful guide to how we and our kids should consume media. Would you mind just walking us through that idea?

Industry observers note that I think the idea of healthy eating is something we understand. The food pyramid, similar to the digital diet pyramid, is weighted with the good nutritious things at the bottom and the not-so-good things, the things that we want to limit, at the top. We might not always choose to follow it. We might sometimes eat a tub of ice cream, but we are aware that we are making that choice. I think what the digital diet pyramid does is it allows people and parents, most particularly, to think about the choices that they are constantly making every time they open a screen. Generally, what we want to do if we want a healthy relationship to screens is we want to be thinking about active, educational, informative, healthy socialization as forming the base of that pyramid. And then farther up the top are things like passive consumption, doom scrolling, short-form, low-quality content that we want to mitigate or moderate to a certain degree.

In the digital pyramid, where do you place movies and cinematic video games? I think, these days, a kid who can watch a full movie or pay attention to hours of plot in one of those cinematic video games kind of has a leg up. Do you agree?

Right. So you are talking about long-form content versus short-form content and how that relates to the development of attention spans and the ability to follow full narratives through. Absolutely, not all screen time is created equal. What we want to be doing, where possible, is, of course, running around outside is normally better, but if you are going to use screens, we want that screen time to ideally be long-form engagement, like good quality movies, where possible, interactive engagement and collective viewing.

In a recent development, so particularly with young children, ideally, you are sitting there with them watching a Julie Andrews movie talking about the content, using it as a springboard for their discussion. If it takes place during World War II, maybe that is a discussion point for you to talk a little bit about history and use the viewing as a jumping-off point for education and for communication. That's where we really want to be with screen consumption, if we are going to be using those screens. Generally, the bigger the screen and the longer the content, the better.

So Mary Poppins over Roblox, that's my takeaway from this.

In a recent development, I appreciate how Smartphone Nation repeats the idea that screens aren't all bad and that the concept of “screen time” can shame parents for turning to screens ever. I think your book is a nice counterpoint to The Anxious Generation’s Jonathan Haidt, which primarily argues that taking away phones and getting kids outside is the answer. You note that being digitally native isn't all bad. So my question for you is, if screen time limits aren't the answer, where should we start?

First, let's talk about where screen time comes from as a concept. Screen time, that guidance came out of some pretty good physical health research, mostly around childhood obesity and childhood diabetes from about 15 years ago. What that research said was, "If kids are sedentary, if they are sitting in front of screens all the time, they aren't moving around, that's bad for their physical health." That is still true. And Jonathan Haidt's argument around that is true. If you are in front of screens, you're not moving around, and that's not good for your physical health and aspects of your mental health, and I absolutely agree with that. But that guidance really just captured the quantity of the screen consumption, and not the quality of the screen consumption. So that guidance is limiting in that it doesn't address the mental health implications of what kids might be consuming on screens.

Industry observers note that as we discussed previously, it's a very different scenario to have a kid watching with their parents Mary Poppins than for them to be alone in their bedroom with headphones on, scrolling through an algorithmically-driven feed. That is qualitatively a very different experience. The sad thing is that a Pew research study has recently pointed out that 89% of kids from the age of 5 are on YouTube now, an algorithmically driven, largely unregulated platform, and I think it's about 81% from the age of 3. Now, most of the discussions that we have at the moment around algorithms, around social media, completely leave out those younger years, and they tend to leave YouTube out of that discussion. But really for a lot of us, well-meaning parents, without realizing it, we're actually grooming our kids into these algorithmically-driven short-form, often low-quality content, from a really early age. So what we need to get to grips of is that not all screen time is equal and that we're actually needing to make an active choice.

It has been revealed that fortunately, there are many more choices available to us as parents than our parents had to make. That's not to say that we weren't plopped in front of screens to watch hours of content with bad-quality TV dinners (we were), but these were different screens and it was different content. Those were largely regulated spaces, often programmed by children's commissioners who were experts in programming children's content that had a diversity of content. You weren't watching 10 episodes of Bluey in a row. Those regulated spaces that a lot of good advocacy went into in order to develop, if we think of the development of children's programming on PBS, unfortunately, a lot of that good work has been thrown out the window because those kids are not on those spaces anymore, they're on YouTube, and that is a great tragedy.

Recent findings suggest that I think it's really vital as parents that we remind ourselves that we are making choices. But because we are making choices, we can make different choices and we can make empowered decisions about the types of screens and the types of digital spaces we want our kids to inhabit. There's great empowerment in that I think.

You just mentioned how even Bluey could be problematic, which I've actually never thought about. It is a really good point. If you give the kid the control or you let it auto-rotate and do eight in a row, Bluey is a completely different experience. Whereas, usually, it's the safest possible space for parents with young kids.

I'm not saying that Bluey is problematic. It's not problematic. What is problematic is allowing a binge watching of an entire season. We actually should be having diversity of content. There are great things about curated spaces, and there are great things about children's programming that has carefully thought through what comes after what and that there's some kind of host that comes in and makes sense of things for kids. Terrestrial TV is a very different experience. When I speak to my kids who are still very little about healthy screen consumption, I talk about terrestrial TV. I talk about algorithms and the fact that algorithms make our choices for us. It's important that we're active in our decision-making and that there are experts and, in the post-truth world, it's worth acknowledging, that there are some people that curate viewing experiences and these are regulated spaces. That means that that's a different experience so that there are healthy forms of screen consumption and less healthy forms of screen consumption.

Now, that is not to say that running around outside is still a much better thing to do. Of course, it is. But if you are going to use a screen, it's good to be much more intentional about how you do it.

Recent findings suggest that if I can move to a slightly older audience. I have a teen myself, so I think about this all the time. How do I stop my kid from getting red-pilled?

When we talk about online extremism or the echo chambers that our kids or our uncles or ourselves might be in, I think it's really important to take a step back and think about the technological processes at play. The reason that young boys are often fed online misogyny or more extreme content is because it is more attention-grabbing. The reason that girls are fed body dysmorphic content and self-harm is because it's more attention-grabbing. The financial structures of social media are an attention economy. The whole system is set up to hold our attention as long as possible and, in fact, hold our attention a little longer each time. Unfortunately, that often means that hate, harm, and disinformation are often algorithmically prioritized because they are more attention-grabbing, because disinformation is often more attention-grabbing than truth.

Recent findings suggest that one of the best things we can do, and we absolutely should be doing this with teenagers, is talking about that concept, talking about the attention economy, talking about the way in which we are manipulated through social media, and our usage and our behaviors online are collected in order to manipulate us, just to hold us a little bit longer. If you talk to kids about this idea, even from early teenage years, they don't like it. They don't like the idea of being emotionally manipulated and controlled. One thing that I talk about with any type of echo chamber is instead of fighting or debating your teenager or uncle at Thanksgiving dinner around the specificity of the problem, around the granular detail. It's better to take a step back, collectivize, and talk about the ways in which these technological and corporate structures are feeding them this content and pushing them potentially down a narrower and narrower path.

And then it becomes you together against those structures, and that becomes a very powerful thing. One, you are equipping your young person with tools to be empowered digital citizens, and, two, it's something you're in together because you yourself are not immune to it and you are probably being fed something different, but it may be something that makes you feel bad.

According to recent reports, this one's for parents of neurodivergent kids. It seems that we are getting pulled in two directions. On one hand, social media is more dangerous. One study you cited said that the likelihood of seeing self-harm content is, tell me if I'm getting this right, 40% greater for those with mental health difficulties, 31% greater for kids with autism. On the other hand, you also write that evidence suggests that screens can provide predictability and a sense of belonging within like-minded communities and can be instrumental in helping neurodiverse kids manage anxiety. Can you please walk us through this?

Sources indicate that I think this goes back to this idea of quality consumption and the choices that we make around our screens. That work around social media-fed harm or algorithmically-prioritized harm and the way in which neurodiverse kids are disproportionately targeted is immensely problematic, and, if you have a neurodiverse child, something you should be aware of. That is not unique to neurodiverse children. Social media is very, very good at predicting our behaviors, but also at knowing our vulnerabilities because it is through those vulnerabilities that it can point out [what we] lack and we are more susceptible to buying things if we feel a lack. That fits into this business model. The work that has been done around the way in which screens can support neurodiversity tends to be around ways in which screens can be used to calm kids, ways in which different learning applications can support neurodiverse kids, and that there are ways in which differently abled kids might find community through the internet. That remains true and those are good things, but of course we're almost talking about different usages of screens. That stuff is not happening on TikTok in the same way. It just really isn't.

Sources indicate that A lot of the discussions that we used to have around the beauty of social media a decade ago and the way it gave platforms for speaking voice and finding community has shifted as the technology has become more and more sophisticated and more and more manipulative. When we talk about that good stuff, we really need to be careful about how we're carving out those spaces, what screens we're using to do them, and where those screens are being used.

In another sense, keep kids away from the algorithms.

Industry observers note that yeah. For younger teenagers, I tend to find that algorithmically driven content is more and more problematic. As these systems become more and more sophisticated, they will be able to hold our kids' eyeballs longer and longer and longer, and we have to push back against that.

In a recent development, it's hard to do forever, of course, even if we hold off social media until they are 16. That birthday will come, and they will turn 17. What we want to be doing is preparing our kids. Just like you would teach them how to drive, you would prepare them and you would talk to them about the dangers and you would talk about how to use it safely.

Hear, hear. You acknowledge throughout this book that so much falls on parents that shouldn't, that the dark recesses of this online culture we're fighting is not our fault, but it is the fault of corporate profits and lack of regulation. What do you say to us burned-out and angry parents? I wonder, you seem so pragmatic, are you angry at all at this world?

Yes, absolutely. I am like an angry mama bear, but I do think that there is power in that anger too and I think a movement is starting. I am hopeful, because if there is enough of us that are angry, we will see change because policy follows the public will. But I do acknowledge that, at the moment, so much is heaped on individual responsibility in a way we don't have for anything else. We're used to consumer protections. We're used to consumer protections around the food we eat, the medication we take, the cars we drive, the small parts on kids' toys so they don't choke. We are used to being protected, and we're not being protected in this space and our kids are not being protected in this space. There is a newness in that. Most things have to be proven safe before they hit the market. For social media, the opposite has been true.

According to recent reports, now, unfortunately, that means that the duty of care and the responsibility is currently falling on us as parents. So while we wait for regulation, while we wait for greater corporate responsibility, we need to know that if our kids are going to inhabit this space, they're doing so without seat belts, and that's why we need to educate ourselves as parents. We need to do that work. I think that doesn't make it our fault. This is not our fault, but we do need to learn these things or else our kids will be forced to navigate it alone.

In a recent development, on the flip side, how do we fight? How should we join the movement? What's your advice for those of us who want the anger to spill out in the public space?

This is why this book is not written in the way that other books are, which is often from a mental health perspective. That's not my expertise. I operate in the digital space. I'm talking about how these technological processes work so that you yourself can be informed about them and you can push back against it. I think if enough people understand that, if enough people read this book, they will say, "This is crazy. This is totally crazy that we've allowed this to happen," and that's when you will see policy change because, ultimately, that's how democracy works. If you think of really successful grassroots movements, it is because people inform themselves and they think it's no longer acceptable.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Buying gifts for tweens and teens can be a special kind of holiday torture.
  • Sources indicate that since many of us on the Scary Mommy team are living with these outspoken arbiters of taste, we’ve done the reconnaissance for you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here are the gifts that’ll actually pass the vibe check.

Buying gifts for tweens and teens can be a special kind of holiday torture. Don’t get us wrong; it’s so much fun when you get it right. But it doesn’t always go that way, largely because their likes and wants are a moving target. Last year they wanted everything from the toy aisle. Now they want... a hoodie? A lip balm that ~everyone~ has? “Just money”? And boy, if you get it wrong, they’ll let you know. (It’s in the eyes.).

Sources indicate that since many of us on the Scary Mommy team are living with these outspoken arbiters of taste, we’ve done the reconnaissance for you. Some of these gifts are cozy staples they’ll wear on repeat until spring, like ultra-soft sweats. Some are creative outlets that aren’t too “kiddish,” like a retro digital camera. And some are the niche little things they’ll be weirdly thrilled to find in their stocking, like cloud-shaped body mists.

Sources indicate that basically, it’s a big ol’ list of things they’ll love... even if they’d never admit it out loud.

This is exactly the kind of open-ended, screen-free creative experience that I actually feel good putting under the tree. The Charmspring Create Kit Enchanted is developed by childhood experts and designed to spark genuine imagination and independent play, which means I hand it over to my daughter and she disappears into her own world for a very satisfying amount of time. — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social.

Recent findings suggest that I got these for my athlete nephew, who had previously informed me that Bruce Bolt is THE BEST brand, full stop. I’ll admit I checked them out when they arrived, and I was seriously impressed by the quality. They feel incredible, look super cool (this electric-pink-aqua-blue combo was my nephew’s top pick), and the super-grippy palm is designed for confident catches. He’s worn these — along with the tackified compression arm sleeves — to his games this season, and swears they’re magic. — Julie Sprankles, Deputy Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment.

These cloud-shaped body mists are cute enough to be a bag charm (trending) but durable enough to stand up to the wear and tear of living on a middle schooler's backpack. The scents are just right for the tween and teen age group too — not too childish, but not too mature either. I gave two of them to my 13-year-old niece, who used them up, and I love them as a stocking stuffer idea! — Katie McPherson, Associate Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment.

Recent findings suggest that in the summer, the teens wear their Birkenstocks, and in the winter they switch to their UGGs — it is just the way of the world. I have declared these shoes too expensive to purchase as regular school clothes, so my daughter has appealed to Santa for help. He obliges. And since my kids also refuse to wear coats all winter, I'm happy to at least get them in some shoes that have a fuzzy lining. And for purchasing, I can't say it enough: Always go through Zappos so you can exchange and return things while dealing with the best customer service ever. — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor, News & Social.

The Huffy GRM is exactly the kind of big holiday gift that makes a kid absolutely lose it on Christmas morning! The 24-inch frame is perfect for older kids ready to upgrade from their first bike, and the GRM has a sleek, sporty look that feels genuinely cool rather than obviously like a kids’ bike. It comes mostly assembled right out of the box so the Christmas morning setup is not a three-hour ordeal, and Huffy has been making reliable, fun bikes for decades at a price point that makes a big gift actually achievable. — Katie Garrity.

My 15-year-old and I are both significant Grace & Stella fans, so we were pumped to try these new Luscious Lip Gloss Butters. They did not disappoint! They glide on smooth and dewy, not sticky, and they smell amazing too. My favorite detail is the little keychain attachment, so my daughter can clip it to her backpack or keys and always have it on hand (read: stop “borrowing” mine). These would make a great stocking stuffer for any tween or teen. — Julie Sprankles.

Seriously, how cute is this? My tween with long, straight hair is ready for her own arsenal of haircare products, and I desperately need her to stop stealing stuff from my bathroom, including my hair dryer. I love how fun this is, I love the accessories, and I love how it's affordable but from a really trusted haircare brand. We went with the pink. — Sarah Aswell.

According to recent reports, for the tween or teen on your list who could use a little support in the self-care and mental wellness department, a Therabox subscription is one of the most thoughtful gifts you can give. Each monthly box is curated by licensed therapists and packed with full-size wellness and self-care products designed to support emotional health, reduce stress, and encourage healthy habits. It arrives like a gift every single month, which makes it the present that keeps going long after the holidays are over, and the therapist-curated angle means every product inside actually has a purpose beyond just smelling nice. It’s a gift that states “I see you and I want you to feel good” in the most tangible way possible! — Katie Garrity.

In a recent development, I have two tweens who are total musicheads, so I knew they’d flip for this Marshall Emberton III portable speaker. It’s a total upgrade from tinny phone audio, with that classic, cool Marshall look and full 360-degree sound. As a mom, I really appreciate that it’s built to handle real life: dustproof, waterproof, and the battery lasts 32+ hours on a single charge. — Julie Sprankles.

It has been revealed that practically every child I know is into some form of lip balm, which is great because personally I didn't discover it until much later in life and now adore it, too. These lip balms make a great stocking stuffer: they're cute, they smell awesome (they come in kid-friendly flavors like "Frosted Sugar Plum" and "Candy Cane Fluff), and they're affordable. Add to cart stat. — Kate Auletta.

Industry observers note that sometimes my teen's Christmas list just looks like a list of hoodies. One of her all-time favorites is this upcoming classic from Hollister. These are super soft and oversized (but not huge), making it easily fall into the "my favorite hoodie" territory. I also bought these for my boy nephews for the holidays — you just really can't go wrong with these, I swear. — Sarah Aswell.

Recent findings suggest that this sleep set has completely changed our bedtime routine. The Dreamjellie pillow is designed specifically for kids and teens, with a shape that supports proper alignment whether they sleep on their side, back, or stomach, and the whole set comes with everything needed for a genuinely cozy, sleep-optimized setup. Getting a tween to actually wind down and sleep well is one of the great challenges of this age, and having bedding that feels special and is actually designed for their bodies makes a real difference. — Katie Garrity.

Sources indicate that this might be the gift that gets the biggest reaction from my gamer teen this year! It snaps right onto their phone and turns it into a handheld gaming console, with full-size joysticks and rear buttons, plus a comfy ergonomic grip. It works with almost any game that supports controllers, from Roblox and Minecraft to Xbox and PlayStation remote play. They can even go wireless and play on a tablet, PC, or TV! My husband fully looks forward to helping my son “test” this out when it comes in. — Julie Sprankles.

I have a feeling many tween girls in my life will live for this gift: It’s a locket and strawberry-scented lipgloss in one. The lip gloss is cruelty-free, nut-free, and gluten-free, and is gentle enough for little kids to use over and over again. I also love that, once the gloss is gone, a message reading “You Are Super!” appears. I couldn’t love this more. — Kate Auletta.

It has been revealed that this is a new brand for me, but they have so many cute, affordable clothes that really seem to speak to my two teen kids. This double-layered shirt creates such a cool look (SO reminiscent of 90s Delia's, by the way), and it doesn't break the bank. I feel like I can buy a few cute shirts from here and make my kid's whole month. — Sarah Aswell.

For the tween or teen who is living on their phone camera but deserves something that actually feels like a real creative tool, the Lola is the answer. The silver color is genuinely stunning and the kind of thing a style-conscious tween will want to carry everywhere and photograph everything with. — Katie Garrity.

Sources indicate that both of my teens love to create fun little skits and videos as a creative outlet, so I figured it was time to get them an actual tripod instead of watching them precariously balance their phones on random objects to get the shot. I like that this one extends up to 71 inches, and that the Bluetooth works from up to 33 feet away. Plus, it folds down to 13 inches and weighs about a pound, making it easy to toss in a backpack. Oh, and it’s super affordable! — Julie Sprankles.

It has been revealed that I’m sort of like a tween in that I, too, live for a ridiculously fun bag. What I love about this is that you can position the bear (it also comes as a panda, unicorn, and fuzzy heart) to look like it's hugging you. It’s completely adorable and makes a great gift for tweens everywhere. — Kate Auletta.

My 11-year-old is an art fanatic, but finding the right kits for her can be hard, as a lot of stuff is a little too "kidish." But she loves these eraser kits by Pretty Pixel, which allow her to either use templates or create her own characters. She loves making erasers for friends or challenging herself to make her favorite anime characters. One thing I love? The kits to buy more eraser materials are super affordable. — Sarah Aswell.

For the Swiftie on your list who has everything, this is the gift that genuinely surprises them. Historic Newspapers compiles real newspaper coverage of Taylor Swift’s career from her earliest days all the way through her record-breaking eras, printed and bound into a beautiful keepsake book that reads like a time capsule of pop culture history. It is the kind of deeply personal, one-of-a-kind gift that no amount of merch shopping replicates, and for a tween or teen who has grown up watching Taylor dominate the world, seeing it all documented in real news print is going to hit differently. — Katie Garrity.

Recent findings suggest that if your teen’s bedroom doubles as a gaming den (hi, my son), let me put you on these Nanoleaf Blocks! They combine customizable smart lighting with shelves and pegboards so your gamer can mix and build a custom wall feature around their PC. They also connect with other Nanoleaf products, so the system can grow with them. But the reactive lighting is the real showstopper: When my son plays a game, the blocks’ lighting shifts to match the colors on his screen, creating a super-cool immersive experience. — Julie Sprankles.

I'm a fan of anything that gets my kids off screens, and this Camp Snap Mini Camcorder did not come to play. It's compact, it's screen-free, and it has point-and-shoot recording (just like the old days!) with five film-inspired filters. There's no playback screen, no Wi-Fi, and no apps required — what a welcome change, huh? Definitely getting this for my older kid for Christmas. — Kate Auletta.

Industry observers note that this brand, SMOKO, has so many cute things that both of my teens would gladly die for. But this couch potato drinking a boba tea? That lets you turn off the overhead lights that my children hate with their whole hearts? Priceless. These are at a great price point, too, for things like friends' birthday gifts. — Sarah Aswell.

Sources indicate that cloud Nine’s sweatpants have a reputation that genuinely precedes them. The fabric is that buttery, weightless softness kids refuse to take off once they put them on, and for a tween with strong opinions about comfort, this is basically a guaranteed win. They are the kind of cozy, elevated loungewear that looks cute enough to wear out but feels good enough to sleep in, which at this age is basically the holy grail of getting dressed. — Katie Garrity.

These I Love Aromie Bakery plushies are adorable and smell SO good. Buying this for my daughter because it combines two things she’s obsessed with, Squishmallows and anything that’s satisfying to squeeze, into one tiny, glittery package. I'm Not A "Bowel Normie" & I Still Have Three Healthy Kids

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1014 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • My body, once a disintegrating and diseased lump of organs, had made so much life.
  • We were on a family trip to Fresh York City to celebrate New Year’s Eve in Times Square.
  • It has been revealed that over the next three years, I spent much of my time in doctor’s offices and bathrooms, with bloating, constipation, diarrhea and bleeding.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

My body, once a disintegrating and diseased lump of organs, had made so much life.

I became sick when I was 12. It happened out of nowhere. We were on a family trip to Fresh York City to celebrate New Year’s Eve in Times Square. I stood out on the Statue of Liberty’s crown, sipping the (extravagantly priced) hot chocolate my parents bought me to combat the cold, gazing in awe at the dazzling metropolis, and was suddenly overcome with nausea. That night, I began vomiting, running to the toilet, and developed a high fever. I couldn’t even make it to the window to see the ball drop.

It has been revealed that over the next three years, I spent much of my time in doctor’s offices and bathrooms, with bloating, constipation, diarrhea and bleeding. I was in pain, mostly searing pangs. Who knew when they would hit? I went for X-rays, scopes, breath tests, physical exams; I tried medications, carbon supplements, acupuncture. Steroids worked miraculously at first, then not at all. Experimental drugs went through me completely undigested. I began to evacuate the lining of my own colon; it looked like a thin white snake. My blood count was so low I was repeatedly hospitalized for blood transfusions and iron infusions. It appeared I had very severe ulcerative colitis.

Industry observers note that during this time, I was in 7th to 10th grades, the time of first loves, frenemies, tattoos and drivers ed. But as someone with acute bowel disease, my teenage life was increasingly limited. Want a ride home? No thanks. I was worried that whoever was driving would take detours, keeping me away from a toilet. The metro was scary; what if it stalled and I was stuck? I went to school but sat next to the door of the classroom. It was hard for me to go to boy-girl get-togethers: I couldn’t even sit through a movie in someone’s basement, and what if the bathroom was within earshot? The logistics were so difficult, the risk of embarrassment too high. I stopped attending most things.

All teenagers deal with their body changing, with it being out of their control. My body was waging war on me, emitting shameful sounds, smells and sights without my consent. It felt like I, Little Judy, was buried somewhere deep inside this morass of sickly flesh, this thing that all these ancient doctors were probing, trying to decipher. Had I done something to cause this? Was it my fault? I didn’t not-love my body, I hated it.

According to recent reports, when my friends were exploring sexuality, I recoiled. For one, it’s hard to think about smooching when you’re doubled down in anguish. Constantly exposed to the medical world, I’d created strong barriers, dissociating from my physical experience.

Not to mention, how could I possibly share what I was going through with anyone? My peers were worried about algebra tests; I was worried about blood tests. My friends gossiped about trying drugs; I was on more drugs than half the school combined! I went to doctors who mentioned the possibility of developing cancer. I felt misunderstood, alone, and so very ugly. I didn’t know how to let anyone get close.

Sources indicate that by tenth grade, my life was completely in the toilet, literally. Surgery was offered as an option. Major surgery: they would remove my entire large intestine colon and create a pouch from part of the small intestine that would, hopefully, work as a de facto colon. Doctors kept postponing the procedure, worried about the risks. But I insisted on the operation. I told my parents, if they didn’t take me, I’d take the bus.

So, at 15, I had my entire colon removed. My pouch was amazing; I was not a “bowel normie,” and I couldn’t eat with abandon, but I lived a mostly pain-free life. I remained relatively healthy through my twenties, eventually dating (and making up for lost time!). I got married at age 31 to a man who I was able to open up to about my chronic condition, and who was willing to support my toilet paper habit. But then came the question: was my body robust enough to have a baby? Could I get past all my shame, all my corporeal disappointment, to create a life? And should I be a parent, i.e. would my children end up sick too? I wobbled for two years.

It has been revealed that then, the second I’d decided to maybe even consider trying to get pregnant, my gynecologist enrolled me in a fertility clinic, saying, “People with your surgeries have so much trouble, there’s not a minute to waste.” A few weeks later, I was doing bloodwork at my local clinic so they could send the results to the fertility center. Only, it turned out, as a squealing nurse revealed, I was already pregnant.

In a recent development, the nine months passed seamlessly, bowel-wise, except for some excruciating bouts of gas that had become trapped under my growing belly. My first daughter was born healthy via C-section (recommended, as natural childbirth carried a risk of damaging the pouch). Though I did have a dangerous and frightening ectopic pregnancy a few years later when trying for my second — most likely due to scar tissue from the old surgery — I ultimately ended up having three children which is a miracle, and also, a little insane. My body, once a disintegrating and diseased lump of organs, had made so much life! Never mind years of yoga and pilates, finally, I felt strong. And even, a little bit beautiful.

Judy Batalion is a New York Times bestselling author of award-winning nonfiction and fiction. Her essays have appeared in The New York Times, The Washington Post, and Vogue, among others. Judy has a BA in the History of Science from Harvard, a PhD from the University of London, and has worked as a museum curator and university lecturer. She lives in New York City with her husband and three children.

#136185. Gary Vaynerchuk Just Wants Us All To Be (And Raise) Nice Guys

📅 13 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2179 w)

Gary Vaynerchuk Just Wants Us All To Be (And Raise) Nice Guys

📅 13 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2179 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “I have all of my validation, and I mean all of it, wrapped up in being a nice guy.”.
  • It has been revealed that if you haven’t seen Louis Theroux: Inside the Manosphere, make a date with Netflix.
  • In a recent development, in the documentary, Theroux, the understated British journalism, calmly and a bit coldly explores the manosphere from the inside.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“I have all of my validation, and I mean all of it, wrapped up in being a nice guy.”.

It has been revealed that if you haven’t seen Louis Theroux: Inside the Manosphere, make a date with Netflix. This is must-see TV for parents, especially parents raising boys. But a word of warning, it’s like a scary movie that will haunt you well after the credits run. Weapons has nothing on the horror show that is the manosphere.

In a recent development, in the documentary, Theroux, the understated British journalism, calmly and a bit coldly explores the manosphere from the inside. In talking to the most extreme influencers — the peddlers in misogyny and anti-semitism, conspiracy and homophobia — he finds himself pulled in to the fight, made into content, taken out of context, and expertly trolled, even as he holds the camera. “He really don’t wanna be in the live,” one such British influencer says to the camera in front of Theroux on a particularly disturbing night out. “He don’t wanna be on the content. But he’s got no choice.”.

In a recent development, we parents, on the other hand, do have a choice — to shield our kids from the depravity, to push back against the cultural creep, and to turn to other influencers. Influencers like Gary Vaynerchuk, the best-selling author, radio host, entrepreneur, and an unabashed dude who plays his part as the antidote to the vitriol of the manosphere. As an executive — CEO of VaynerMedia and Chairman of VaynerX — he’s a hard-nosed, fast-talking entrepreneur who believes in bootstrapping life. He also fundamentally believes in kindness. “I know I was well parented,” he tells Fatherly, “and I have all of my validation, and I mean all of it, wrapped up in being a nice guy.”.

Parents can choose to be nice, sure, but Vaynerchuk also notes we can choose to be more accountable, to stop coddling our kids on one hand while taking charge on the other (taking away their social media access or phones if we need to). “Supporting your child is everything,” claims Vaynerchuk. “Enabling your child is a disaster.” And walking that tightrope between the two? That’s parenting.

The following interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

Industry observers note that gary Vaynerchuk is an unapologetically wealthy entrepreneur. But his empasis on self-improvement and kindness poses an key question: What’s the point of being rich if you’re an unhappy jerk?

What do you think is the real reason people are checking out — from the workforce but also social life — and how can we inoculate our kids, and especially boys, against this?

Gary Vaynerchuk: I think modern parenting has lost its way. I think we've made a couple of crucial mistakes, and we're blaming it on social media because we don't like accountability. Mistake number one: I do think, especially for boys, we got a little too into eighth-placed trophies, a little too "fighting isn't the way to resolve things", a little too coddle-y-coddle-y. Listen, I'm a mama's boy through and through. I also got into ten fights in school, and my mom had no opinions about it, meaning it was like, "Yeah, life." I think we've gotten too in our kids' business. Again, everyone grows up in different circumstances. There's plenty of kids right now that don't have parents in their business.

According to recent reports, forget about the '80s and '90s. From the '70s and '60s, '50s and '40s, '30s and '10s, '00s, and on back to the 1800s … parents did not go to school and yell at teachers for giving their kid a B instead of an A. But that is what has happened the last 20 years. ... The f*ck are we texting our sons who are 27 because we have the family f*cking strategy and knowing where everyone is? Let men be men.

Who do you think wins in a fight: a lion that grew up in the Bronx Zoo, or a lion in the jungle?

We've raised a lot of zoo lions in the last 25 years. We need to take a little bit of our foot off the pedal.

What role do you think sports play in teaching some of this wildness, some of this conflict?

I think it's everything. When my son was growing up, during a game, if there was a kid that cried when they lost, I used to, with the parents' permission, I would be like, "It's good that you're crying kid. Don't listen to your parents." Multiple parents were happy that I was doing that for their kid.

Industry observers note that I think if you have a kid that cries when they lose in sports, you've been given a blessing. And I think you should compound that, not suppress it. Teaching your kids that nothing matters is a bad idea — leads to depression. If someone remarked to me around a game of monopoly tonight, "Bro, it's just a game." I'd be like, "F*ck you, man. This is life. When I play, I'm playing for life." So I think sports is everything, but I think parents get involved too much yelling at the coach. Let the coach cook — even if the coach sucks.

According to recent reports, let [your kid] deal with a sucky coach, because you're going to have a sucky boss. Dad's going to have a sucky day. You're going to have a sucky governor one day in your life. Get used to people that have authority or leverage over you. You're going to interact with a sucky policeman. You're going to have a sucky doctor. You have f*cking 27-year-old men throwing temper tantrums because they never were taught how to deal with sucky authority.

Recent findings suggest that talk to me about humility. How do we get more of it?

Recent findings suggest that sports is where I learned humility, and it is my superpower. My mom would've not raised a humble child. I thought I was Superman. I literally thought I was the most athletic and most handsome person on earth somewhere around fourth grade. Because in my neighborhood, I had the best hand-eye coordination. And in my neighborhood, I was a little bit better athletically … I won a lot, and then it started to change. And that was a rude awakening. I mean, going through the journey of humility, first getting used to the taste.

I would lose, play again. I would lose, play again. I annoyed people. I feel it's now coming clear to me, literally in real time right now with you, I feel like in second, third, fourth grade, I might've had excuses. So it took some time to acquire that taste, but much like caviar, much like sweetbreads and truffles … oysters, that initial [taste] is like, "Oh, it's a little weird.".

And now I love the acquired taste. [Similarly] I now love humility. I love it. It got me here. And now that I'm, quote-unquote, "at some level of success", and I know people look at me, I love that the kids see my humility in meetings behind the scenes. I hope it inspires them to realize it's a beautiful trait, not a loser trait.

You recognize losing is learning. There's a sweetness to that.

Brother, I'm a little bit even weirder. I like losing. I swear to God, I like it, man. I like adversity. I like it. I'm addicted to the underdog, when someone's an underdog, and then they become the champ. Or the reverse; Kobe, Tiger Woods. Tiger, early, loved, loved [them] early. But then I was like, when he was the main guy, I was like, "Ah.".

Sources indicate that I’d like to jump into something you've said before and my wife and I use it a lot: "Your kid is not your friend." I have a teen right now. I think that truth has kind of hit me hard fairly recently. Do you still believe that, and why? What's the motivation behind it? What's the evidence?

I mean, the evidence is I'm 50 fucking years old and I get 10,000 DMs a day, and I read the content, and I analyze the content. If you're not the person for your child that teaches consequences and ramifications, it's going to be a problem. They'll learn it. Life will teach them, starting at 22, which ... F*ck, man, to unlearn 22 years of that behavior ...

Sources indicate that listen, supporting your child is everything. Enabling your child is a disaster, and that is a fine f*cking line. It's been amazing in so many ways to watch the generation of women that are [now] 48-years-old and are straight best friends with their 15-year-old daughter. Kids are older, and parents are younger, so it makes sense to me. I think it's actually beautiful, but I think there's a lot of moms who lose the plot in the beauty of ... the nirvana of such a gorgeous relationship, and I think they feel the ramifications later, and they need to be eyes wide open.

Being friendly is amazing. You know [parents tell me], "No, Gary, you don't get it. I want them to come to me. I couldn't go to my mom." Yeah, your mom was treating you inappropriately too far in the other direction, but they come to you because you're their f*cking drug dealer. You're dealing the drug of non-accountability. You're dealing the drug of no consequences. You're giving them a little hit of, "It's everyone else's fault but yours.".

According to recent reports, I'm wondering how that practically plays out when it comes to money. How do you teach your kids about money, the hustle, the passion, work?

Sources indicate that very easy. You stop giving it to them. And the question becomes, when? I have a big thing of 15, 16, 17, 18 feels in the right range. My parents make fun of me on this. If they watch this, they'll call me and be like, "Eh, eight, nine, seven, 10." They were earlier. But, man, I will say, and this is tough, because I know a lot of dads are going to hear this, if you have a 23-year-old son who you're giving money to, you are destroying that child. They have to stand on their own two feet financially. Look, the old days, AKA the '80s and '90s, kids did borrow money from parents to get their first home, but they paid them back … with interest. That's a foreign concept.

Let me just drop the atomic bomb on everyone that I unearthed eight years ago. I started getting these weird DMs and messages from guys who were 25 sh*tting on their parents for giving them money. I didn't understand, brother. I really didn't. I have the humility to say that the first couple times I read stuff that was similar to this, it just wasn't on my radar yet.

Let me get you all to the punchline: If you have a 27-year-old right now that you're giving money to, he's saying all the right things to you in your face, but let me tell you what he's thinking at 11:00 at night when he takes his second Tito's on the rocks: he thinks that you think he's a loser.

Sources indicate that he's taking it because he wants to keep up with the Joneses. He wants to be able to take his girl on a date. He wants to go on vacation. He wants to get a nice TV in his pad. He wants to have an Equinox membership. He wants to have Uber. He wants to have Starbucks. But I'm telling you, through your actions, are saying to him that you don't respect him as a man.

In a recent development, because he's not independent of you. The focus should be on independence, right?

Industry observers note that I don't think this is red-pilled or anything. A man at 27 should be providing for, minimally, himself, however humble he lives. I lived in a sh*tty apartments with four friends in college because I used my money, even in college.

And it helps us for peace of mind, not financial success. I'm aware that I'm a public businessman, but when I talk about success and winning, I talk about peace of mind, lack of anxiety, not being in depressive moments. I don't know if you not paying for your kid is going to make them financially successful. I do know it's going to make them a man. I just did another podcast earlier. I'm doing a bunch today. Someone said, "Who do you admire?" I said, "Somebody that works two jobs and takes care of their family, and doesn't complain.".

According to recent reports, I admire a man or a woman that provides for their family financially on backbreaking effort without a peep of complaining. Boy, do I put that person on a pedestal. And you add nice? Nice? That’s ultimate.

Digital Detox Gift Guide: 27 Analog Gift Ideas For Lo-Fi Fun

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2369 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From paint-by-numbers to screen-free storytelling, these picks make downtime feel intentional and joyful.
  • Sources indicate that we started noticing it last year: Everyone seemed to be craving less screen time, less doomscrolling, fewer cheap dopamine hits.
  • After all, there’s just a special, cozy kind of magic in a night with no screens, isn’t there?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From paint-by-numbers to screen-free storytelling, these picks make downtime feel intentional and joyful.

Sources indicate that we started noticing it last year: Everyone seemed to be craving less screen time, less doomscrolling, fewer cheap dopamine hits. And not only has that trend continued in 2026, but it’s gotten even stronger. If anything, we’re all more fried! So analog is having a full-blown moment, which happily makes for some seriously great gifting.

After all, there’s just a special, cozy kind of magic in a night with no screens, isn’t there? A puzzle spread across the dining room table. A record spinning while parents dance in the kitchen (and their kids feign disgust in the background). Coloring and baking and crafting and playing board games — comfortcore activities that keep hands busy and minds engaged.

Industry observers note that so this holiday season, give the gift of logging off. From paint-by-numbers to an heirloom-quality chess set, here are our favorite picks for anyone (yourself included) who’s ready to put the phone in a drawer and be fully present for all the holiday merriment.

It has been revealed that turn off the TV and start a puzzle! And thanks to Completing The Puzzle, you no longer have the excuse, “But I don't know what to do with it when I'm done!” They've figured that all out for you. Completing The Puzzle is the first-ever puzzle rental subscription with high-quality puzzles delivered right to your door. Once you finish, pack it up, send it back, and wait for your new one to arrive. — Kate Auletta, Editor in Chief.

Sources indicate that I have stated for about 100 years that I wanted to get into embroidery. Whenever I see something embroidered at an antique mall or thrift store, I am enchanted, but... they are not cheap. Even thrifted! So, why not make my own? Clever Poppy is the perfect way to get an introduction to embroidery if you're a newbie like me. In their kits, they provide step-by-step instructions as well as everything you need to get started. — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social.

Normalize getting your mom a knit or crochet kit! If they like fiber arts, they will love it. Sometimes people gift me a few balls of yarn, which is amazing, but these kits ensure that I have enough to complete a project. I love Lion Brand's selections, and this cardigan is gorgeous and pretty easy to pull off, too! — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor, News & Social.

There’s something so deeply satisfying about dropping the needle on a record. You can’t skip songs, you can’t scroll... you actually listen to an album in its purest form. This record player makes that ritual easy, and it looks good doing it with its cool retro-inspired case and little viewing window. It plays both LPs and singles, and it’s compact enough to move wherever you want. I can’t wait to hit the local thrift stores and start building my vinyl collection. (Worth noting: This turntable does also have Bluetooth!) — Julie Sprankles, Deputy Editor of Lifestyle & Entertainment.

For all the readers out there, this is one book accessory I never knew I needed! I throw my book into my bag along with all my other crap and typically end up ruining it with crayon marks or crumbs from my kid's latest half-eaten snack. This protective padded sleeve keeps your current reads safe from crushed pages and bent covers (and mystery stains!). — Katie Garrity.

In a recent development, coloring girlies, if you're not using Ohuhu markers, we need to talk! This 104-color pack is my go-to when I'm having a cozy coloring night with my daughter. Plus, these markers have a dual-tip marker design — choose the brush tip for sweeping, calligraphic strokes, or the fine tip for details. — Katie Garrity.

Sources indicate that I’ve got nothing against my Notes app. In fact, I use it all the time. But I will always, always be a girlie who loves a really beautiful notebook and the way it makes me want to put down my phone and pick up a pen. This journal has a hard cover that comes in some really saturated, beautiful colors; I have the Mulberry and love it, but this Deep Indigo is next on my list! Little thoughtful details just make the notebook a joy to use: thick pages, a ribbon bookmark, a built-in pen holder, and a handy inner pocket. — Julie Sprankles.

According to recent reports, for the person on your list who has approximately 10,000 photos living in their phone and zero prints to show for it, a Mixbook photo book is the most meaningful and genuinely beautiful gift you can give. Mixbook is consistently rated one of the best photo book services for quality and customization, with hundreds of gorgeous themes and layouts that make the final product look intentional and special rather than just a dump of your camera roll. The design tool is incredibly easy to use, the printing quality is stunning, and they run sales constantly, which makes a truly luxurious gift very achievable. — Katie Garrity.

Anyone who has an addiction to making sourdough (or eating it like me) will absolutely love this bread bag from Keeki. It’s a beeswax-lined linen bag that stores your loaf and allows the bread to breathe. The natural antibacterial properties of beeswax will help deter mold! — Katie Garrity.

I’ve long been a fan of Papier, so I was pumped to see the brand venture into board games, starting with this gorgeous Midnight Mosaic Chess Set. It has a scalloped (!!) solid wood board with a full set of wooden pieces, plus a harlequin-patterned box pretty enough to live right on my coffee table. It’s more of a splurge than I’d normally spend on a board game, but I’m very into the idea of a set that lasts for years... something I can play with my kids now, that I hope they’ll ask to pull back out when they’re off at college and come home for a visit. — Julie Sprankles.

I wouldn't call myself an artist by any means, so that's why a paint-by-numbers kit is perfect. I get the zen of coloring, but the end product is pre-made to be gorgeous! — Katie Garrity.

In a recent development, for the book lover who’s trying to put down the phone, this is Chutes and Ladders with a literary twist, played on a gorgeous bookshelf board illustrated by Hyesu Lee, where ladders send you up and bookmark ribbons slide you back down (instead of snakes). It’s easy enough for little kids and charming enough for adults, with four wooden game pieces and two dice for 2 to 4 players, so it’s a great pick for family game night. It’s the kind of analog gift that actually gets pulled out and played, and it looks too pretty to hide in a closet! — Katie Garrity.

I am just now really getting into Pilates, and I feel like it’s such a top-tier analog activity. No screens, no notifications. Just me and my breath (and my very shaky core, ha). These Fraise socks make the practice a little more luxe! They have a non-slip grip that actually sticks, compression arch support, odor-resistant organic cotton, and a really cute aesthetic, too. But what I REALLY love is that this minority-woman-owned organization donates a pair of socks to local women’s shelters for every order. — Julie Sprankles.

For the adult who needs a break from wrapping presents, this spiral-bound activity book is basically Highlights for Children, but with a lot more sarcasm and a festive attitude. It has 200 pages of hidden-picture puzzles, mazes, coloring pages, connect-the-dots, festive sudoku, and word searches, all printed on uncoated paper that’s great for pens or pencils, with an answer key in the back so no one has to suffer. It’s a screen-free, hilariously unproductive gift that makes a great stocking stuffer for anyone who needs a place to hide from the relatives! — Katie Garrity.

It has been revealed that for the sports fanatic who already owns every jersey and mug, these books are a screen-free gift that relives their team’s biggest games, seasons, and championships through the real newspaper coverage printed at the time. They come in football, baseball, basketball, hockey, soccer, and more, and you can customize each one by choosing the cover color and design, adding their name to the front, and writing your own dedication inside. It’s an analog gift that feels personal and gets proudly displayed on the coffee table instead of shoved in a drawer! — Katie Garrity.

Sources indicate that these Matryoshka measuring cups just make me smile! The design is whimsical and charming, but also super practical: Each cup in the set of six stands upright, nests neatly inside the next, and measures from 1/4 cup to a full cup. They’re great for spending time baking with the kids! — Julie Sprankles.

Recent findings suggest that if you want to romanticize the analog life, this is the pen that does it, because writing with a solid 14K gold nib feels nothing like a regular pen, and the smoothness alone makes grocery lists feel like an entire event. The weighty metal body in matte black was designed by Mario Bellini and has a grooved texture that’s as satisfying to hold as it is to look at, and it comes with a converter and an ink cartridge so you can start writing right out of the box. It’s the kind of pen that gets you to slow down, pick up a notebook, and actually put thoughts on paper, which feels like the whole point of an analog gift guide! — Katie Garrity.

My idea of a perfect night is analog all the way: a puzzle on the table, no screens, and something truly cozy to curl up under. The stone-washed 100% cotton has that already-broken-in softness, and the tonal embroidered leaf design makes it look gorgeous without feeling fussy. It’s lightweight enough that you won’t overheat but still warm enough for a long puzzle session, and it comes with a quilt plus two matching shams to make the whole bed look put together. — Katie Garrity.

Sources indicate that nothing, and I repeat nothing, gets my family to put their phones down faster than the promise of melty marshmallows and chocolate atop graham cracker squares. I love that this Solo Stove S’mores Bundle makes real s’mores possible anywhere! It comes with a tabletop fire bowl, roasting sticks, fuel, and a bamboo tray to hold all the fixings, so you can set up your s’mores station anywhere from the kitchen counter to the coffee table for movie night. There’s even a fun little recipe book with creative riffs on the classic. — Julie Sprankles.

Industry observers note that this is such a perfect gift for a music lover. You connect it to your phone and it displays the album cover of whatever song you're listening to. In a world where we aren't listening to music as thoughtfully as we used to, I love how this brings you back to the days when you would hold and see an album before you played it. This is the perfect gift for the millennial in your life who likes the way we used to do things. — Sarah Aswell.

Industry observers note that tried and true! You cannot go wrong with a good LEGO set, and this one is a classic in our house. I have it in a real vase on my desk, and it just looks so cute. — Katie Garrity.

In a recent development, there is something so nostalgic and special about instant cameras. There's such a sense of joy in seeing a photo printed out on photo paper instead of collecting digital dust in your phone's camera roll. Bring this as a hostess gift to your next event, and I promise, everyone will be fighting over it. — Katie Garrity.

These coloring books are so special for so many reasons. First, the firm proudly donates 10% of all proceeds to animal rescue and rehabilitation efforts, helping more dogs find the love, safety, and second chances they deserve. Secondly, these images are based on the founder's own dogs! — Katie Garrity.

It has been revealed that welp, it’s finally happening: I’m late to the party, but I’m finally hopping on the mahjong train thanks to this limited-edition holiday set. Wildwonder teamed up with AAPI artist Joy Cho of Oh Joy, and her vibrant style really shines through here: The whole thing is stunning and cool and creative. Inside are 160 extra-thick, hand-painted tiles, plus dice and a Birdie Bam tile. Bonus: It comes with a six-pack of Wildwonder sparkling drinks, which are delish (the Mango Gold is my fave). — Julie Sprankles.

One of our favorite things to do as a family is family read-a-thons in the living room: We all grab a blanket and our favorite book. My daughter now begs me to bring out her adorable air mattress for a whimsical, super-cozy feel during our read-a-thons. It's even more magical under the Christmas tree lights! — Katie Garrity.

If you're looking to get your kid off screens, the Yoto Player is our go-to. Our daughter absolutely loves hers. They have hundreds of cards to choose from (stories, music, etc.), plus radio stations and special podcasts. We have both sizes (we love the smaller Yoto for on-the-go), and prefer this over other screen-free media-type toys. — Katie Garrity.

I didn’t get into bread baking during the pandemic, when it was all anyone talked about, but better late than never! I adore the idea of pulling a fresh-baked loaf of bread out of the oven, and I can’t think of a prettier way to do it than with this enameled cast-iron bread loaf oven. This dark red color is SO dreamy! I also like that you can use it for roasting recipes, and that it comes with a solid-wood trivet to rest on for easy oven-to-table serving. — Julie Sprankles.

What Gut Health Actually Means, In A World Where The Algorithm Is Constantly Shilling Supplements

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1134 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what experts actually look for, recommend, and see as red flags.
  • It has been revealed that nervous system regulation, sleepmaxxing, high-functioning burnout — there is always some hot upcoming health topic du jour.
  • In a recent development, we’ve heard the term; what does it actually mean?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what experts actually look for, recommend, and see as red flags.

It has been revealed that nervous system regulation, sleepmaxxing, high-functioning burnout — there is always some hot upcoming health topic du jour. While there’s usually some kernel of true health information buried in the hype, it’s hard to parse what really matters from all the social media “gurus” shilling supplements at the link in bio. This is especially true of “gut health,” a topic that feels like it has dominated wellness spaces for the past few years but also never really comes up in your primary care doctor’s office. So, what does gut health actually mean, particularly for women? What do we need to know, and what is social media fluff?

In a recent development, we’ve heard the term; what does it actually mean? In general, gut health refers to the state of your gastrointestinal tract and how it’s working for you, according to the American Medical Association (AMA). Regular bowel movements, no persistent pain or bloating — these are signs things are going well. Medically speaking, good gut health doesn’t mean you’ve somehow optimized your microbiome (more on that in a minute); it means your digestive tract is functioning as it should, you’re absorbing the nutrients you need, and you’re comfortable throughout the process.

According to recent reports, “I think that it looks different for everybody, but when I have a healthy gut, I feel better overall in my day-to-day life. It’s no bloating on a consistent basis. It’s having regular bowel movements. I’m not racing to the bathroom with loose stools or, on the other side of it, I’m not going days constipated. I don’t feel that brain fog. I have energy, and I’m sleeping well,” claims Chloe Melas, NBC News correspondent and author of The Girl’s Guide to Guts, who lives with ulcerative colitis, a type of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).

Yes, it is a real thing and the subject of reams of medical research.

According to recent reports, inside your intestines live trillions of microorganisms that have a surprising impact on our overall health. According to The Cleveland Clinic, they help break down our food, support our immune systems, and may even play a role in mood and behavioral health. There’s no one perfect gut microbiome either, according to the AMA. Each person’s is unique and depends on their age, diet, medications, genetics, where they live, and more.

It’s normal to have an off tummy day every now and then, sure, but from her own experience and speaking with experts while writing her book, Melas knows there are certain red flags women should watch for when it comes to their gut health.

Recent findings suggest that “If you’re having blood in your stool on a consistent basis, and that more than a handful of times, you need to go see a doctor immediately. That can look like going to see your primary care. Personally, in my experiences in writing this book and interviewing so many different experts, and just what I've gone through in my own life having IBD, I’d say go straight to a gastroenterologist,” Melas indicates.

Recent findings suggest that vomiting, unexplained weight loss, chronic stomach pain, and difficulty swallowing are also red flags, per the AMA. Inconsistent bowel movements, whether that means racing to the bathroom multiple times a day or being chronically constipated, are another reason to schedule an appointment with your doctor, she adds. Cramping, painful bloating, or looking pregnant after eating a meal — these things are not normal, says Melas.

It has been revealed that ignoring early signs of GI issues can keep you from feeling your best, and in some cases, missing a diagnosis you need. Women are twice as likely as men to have IBS, according to the American College of Gastroenterology.

Sources indicate that “For so long, so many of us have just sort of been like, ‘This is just the way life is.’ I think that as women, we just don’t prioritize our health like we should, especially when it comes to our gut health. We’re really good about getting our mammograms and talking about our breast health. We are now finally talking about perimenopause and those symptoms. But 45 million Americans suffer from IBS. Nearly 4 million Americans suffer from inflammatory bowel disease, which raises your chances of having colon cancer. And these are things that require a doctor to help you diagnose.”.

Recent findings suggest that probiotic sodas, gummies, powders... what do experts say will actually help improve your GI health and comfort? What will actually make your microbiome happy, and what’s not worth the money? Health experts agree that a diet rich in fiber is the best way to support your gut’s health.

“I had the privilege of interviewing Dr. William Lee, and he wrote a famous book called Eat to Beat Disease. He noted that you have 39 trillion different bacteria that live inside your microbiome and that you need this gut diversity to have overall good health, and that it really just comes down to having a diverse plate every day when you’re sitting down for your meals,” Melas indicates.

It’s generally recommended for adults to consume 25 to 30 grams of fiber per day, which Melas admits can be hard sometimes with diet alone. That may mean a fiber supplement is worth the investment for you, or it may mean snacking on more fruits and veggies throughout the day where you can.

“We all get so overwhelmed; we’re constantly being targeted by drink this, eat that, take this supplement, take these vitamins. But Dr. Lee says that really what you need is in the front of the grocery store. It's the fruits, it's the vegetables, and that it's the things that are easiest to reach first,” Melas adds.

Ultimately, Melas says she wants more women to prioritize their health, and not to be embarrassed or afraid to talk to their providers about GI health specifically.

“If you are not having regular bowel movements, and by that I mean a massive, beautiful, healthy poop every single day, then something is off with your gut health, full stop, and you need to get it figured out,” she indicates. “If you are bloated all the time, if you feel like every time you eat that cheese or a certain meal that you all of a sudden look like you’re three months pregnant, you’re not imagining it and you’re not crazy. We’ve just been told for so long to normalize it, and it's embarrassing, and it's not sexy, and who wants to sit around with your girlfriends at night and talk about the consistency of your stools? But we need to be talking about it because, honestly, it could save lives.”.

#136179. Breaking: “Do I Have To Go To College?”

Breaking: “Do I Have To Go To College?”

📅 04 May 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1106 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The author of 'Go The F*ck to College' explores the pride and pain of sending your kid out into the world on their own, once and for all.
  • Recent findings suggest that for parents of sleepless young ones, the celebrity of Adam Mansbach is hard to overstate.
  • My heart rate soared as I typed an answer: I mean, we already bought the sweatshirts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The author of 'Go The F*ck to College' explores the pride and pain of sending your kid out into the world on their own, once and for all.

Recent findings suggest that for parents of sleepless young ones, the celebrity of Adam Mansbach is hard to overstate. Bleary-eyed and maybe a little despairing, that first time a parent picks up his tome Go the F*ck to Sleep can be a little transcendent. The irreverent picture book perfectly captures the complex feelings we all experience with toddlers — of being trapped in an exhausting simmering pot of cuddles and dependence and sweetness and frustration. Mansbach let it boil over and we parents found a cathartic laugh. 15 years later, Mansbach is tapping once again into the impossible feelings of parents who are about to send off their children — now teens — to the world, to college. Go the F*ck to College, which is available now everywhere you gets books, is just as sweet, sardonic, and endearingly cathartic as Go the F*ck to Sleep. Even for those of us with pre-teens, it’s a wonderful reminder that the parenting journey is long and fraught, difficult and beautiful — and that it would do use good to find a little humor in it. Here, Adam Mansbach reflects, with fewer curse words and no pictures, on the swirling state he finds himself in as he grapples with just how ready his child is to embark on their own into the world. - Tyghe Trimble, Fatherly.

Do I really have to go to college?

My heart rate soared as I typed an answer: I mean, we already bought the sweatshirts. (Those sweatshirts say Bard College – their dream school, to which they'd been accepted months earlier. We bought like twelve of them.).

But you know I'm in favor of a gap year, I added. What are you thinking?

Recent findings suggest that I just want to live at home. I could be a barista.

Fine with me, I said, trying to play it cool.

Market's kind of saturated, I replied. You'd be better off selling tomatoes.

Hahahahahahaha, I wrote, not laughing.

Thank you for being so supportive, Vivien wrote back. That was heartwarming. Ur f*cking lying, bro.

The thing is, I wasn't lying. I wish I had been, but my excitement, my racing heart, my fake nonchalance — they were all because my true (and truly embarrassing) reaction was Yesssssss! They're not leaving! Everything can stay the same forever! In that moment, I was perfectly willing to trade the exultation I felt when I thought about all the ways Vivien's world was about to get beautifully big for the safe, the familiar, and unlimited free lattes.

It was a good reminder that parenting is all about embracing paradox. If you can't hold opposite ideas in your mind, you might go insane.

When your kids are small, the paradoxes are simple – being consumed with blinding rage when their refusal to go to sleep leaves you trapped in a two-hour snuggle with the person you love most, for example, as I wrote about in a little book called Go the F*ck to Sleep.

A decade later, the paradox might be wrapping your head around the fact that a twelve-year-old is sometimes eighteen and sometimes six – or, as a friend of mine summarized the middle school parenting experience, f*ck you, tuck me in. By high school, it's the realization that the only thing more infuriating than seeing your kid lost in their phone is texting them and not getting a reply within four nanoseconds.

Industry observers note that and as the clock ticks down on graduation, adulthood, independence, the paradoxes grow thornier. For me — beyond the interplay of exultation and melancholy that turned an April Fools joke inside out, or the complexity of letting my kid know they can always come home while also informing them that I'm turning their bedroom into a gym — the biggest paradox is wanting to do the most parenting when the least is needed.

Sources indicate that the moment I realized I could no longer solve all Vivien's problems stands out vividly in my mind. It was fourth grade, and their favorite teacher had announced that she was leaving the school. Vivien felt betrayed and crushed — and because I was powerless to affect the situation, I did something I find far more difficult: sat and listened and went through it with them. However, because I am solution-oriented, or a knucklehead, or because I hate to see my kids in pain, the lesson didn't stick. And so year after year, I've erred on the side of saying here's what you need to do instead of that sounds hard and I'm sure you'll figure it out.

Recent findings suggest that eventually, I got a little better at it. And Vivien turned out capable and resourceful anyway — not least because I taught them to stand up to overbearing authority figures, by which I mean me. But now, with college looming, I find myself scrambling to impart all the wisdom I've grown wise enough to shut up and keep to myself. The problem is, it's either stuff they already know ("No pills, no powders"), precious nuggets that reveal themselves as idiotic the second I say them out loud ("take classes about things you think are interesting!") or jewels whose importance are rivaled only by the impossibility of trying to turn them into prescriptive advice ("learn to quickly discern who is a trustworthy friend who will push you to be the best version of yourself and who is drawn to you because they're an emotional vampire and you're an emotional blood source!").

So as tempted as I am, I'm not giving my kid a last-minute crash course in everything before I drop them off at college. These final months are no time to establish a latest exercise routine or learn basic auto maintenance; they're about enjoying each other's company and purchasing copious bedding. College is the crash course in everything, and nobody's a finished product — not Vivien at eighteen, not me at forty-nine. And maybe the paradox that matters most is that your kid is still your kid even when they're on their own. Or perhaps it's that we grow from the inside out; more than anything, I want Vivien to hold tight to their kidness — the wonder, the silliness, the simple but beautiful moral code they learned in preschool — as they take those first steps into adulthood.

Besides, somebody else at Bard will probably know how to change a tire.

3 Ways To Stop Your Kid From Being A Walking Petri Dish, Per A Pediatrician
