Legend has it that one of my earliest gardening forays involved a large lavender bush. As a toddler, I fell sideways into a mound of perfumed purple blooms and just lay there on my back, gazing at the bobbling petals, apparently with a look of absolute joy on my face. As a grown-up, the joy of lavender is still very much a thing. I may try to be more careful about where I stand these days, but my fascination with this sun-kissed fragrant icon is only getting more pronounced with time.

Few garden pleasures rival the velvety fix of fingers dancing along a billowing carpet of lavender wands on a languid summer afternoon. Beyond its timeless fragrance, lavender offers constant, lyrical movement and enduring cottage garden prettiness that seems to work in a range of palettes and plant combinations. Throw in a chorus of bumblebees drunk on nectar and swinging on those violet spires, and you can see why it’s so easy to fall head over heels for this Mediterranean beauty.

It has been revealed that bizarrely, lavender has a bit of a reputation for being tricky to grow, but the truth is that it’s the ultimate garden rebel. While many perennials long for luxuriant loam and scoops of compost, lavender is sculpted by lean, rocky soils and blistering sun, and it isn’t that hard to harness its intoxicating essential oils and maintain a tight, sturdy habit. Whether you want a petite purple knot garden or a sun-drenched lavender planter, this enduring favorite deserves a spot in every yard. Here’s how to ensure your plants return year after year with lush, aromatic blooms.

It has been revealed that lavandula spp. (L. angustifolia, L. stoechas, L. dentata, L. × intermedia).

Woody sub-shrub / evergreen perennial.

1-3 feet (30-90cm) depending on species.

Well-drained, sandy, gravelly, or gritty loam (pH 6.5-7.5, alkaline-leaning).

USDA zones 5-10 (Not in the US? Convert your zone).

Spring-Summer (May-September, varies by species).

Mediterranean basin, southern Europe, northern Africa, southwest Asia, and the Arabian Peninsula.

Before picking a planting site, you need to distinguish between the main primary cultivated types of lavender. While all share an aromatic character and a love for gritty soil, their hardiness, bloom windows, and fragrance profiles differ. Decide whether you need cold-hardy sweetness, early theatrical blooms, or sweeping garden drama. Matching the type to your USDA zone and regional climate is your first step toward lasting vigor.

Sources indicate that giving lavender the right start is key to years of aromatic, low-maintenance beauty. The ideal planting window depends on your local climate. In cold-winter regions (zones 5-7), set plants in the ground in mid-to-late spring, once all threat of frost has passed. This gives their relatively fragile roots a full growing season to establish before winter freezes arrive. Conversely, in warm southern and western areas (zones 8-10), you need to plant in fall to take advantage of cooling air temperatures while the soil remains warm, letting roots settle without heat stress.

It has been revealed that whatever your zone, give your lavender plenty of elbow room. Crowding traps stagnant humidity around the foliage, encouraging fungal leaf blight. Space standard English varieties and compact hedges 2-3 feet (60-90cm) apart. Give larger hybrid lavandins a generous 3 to 4 feet (90-120cm) of breathing room. If in doubt, grab a Stanley Fatmax Tape Measure from The Home Depot to ensure you give your plants enough room to maintain their crisp notes and elegant shapes.

Industry observers note that when lifting young specimens from nursery pots, resist the urge to vigorously tease apart the root ball. Lavender has a sensitive root network and resents rough handling. Loosen the outer circling root tips gently before settling the plant into place.

To understand what lavender craves, picture a craggy Mediterranean hillside: crumbly, sun-baked, and full of stones. Heavy, water-retentive clay is lavender’s nemesis. If your native soil feels sticky or drains poorly after rain, avoid adding fine builder’s sand, which binds with clay particles to form an impenetrable barrier. Instead, work in generous amounts of coarse horticultural grit, pumice, perlite or crushed gravel. You can buy pouches of Plantonix Organic Perlite from Amazon.

According to recent reports, also, if your soil leans on the acidic side (typical in piney or damp eastern backyards), dust the planting area with some garden lime to lift the soil pH and make it more alkaline. While Spanish lavender is slightly more forgiving of neutral soils, English varieties won’t compromise. When in doubt, build a gentle mound or raised mound bed. Elevating roots even 6 inches (15cm) can make a world of difference.

Lavender is a lusty sun-lover that doesn’t want to compromise on light. To maintain high concentrations of aromatic essential oils, these plants need a minimum of 6 hours of direct, unfiltered sunlight daily, with 8 or more hours preferred. Planting in partial shade can lead to leggy growth, sparse flowering, and floppy support.

It has been revealed that position your lavender along a south or west-facing brick wall, a flanking stone path, or nestled beside a gravel terrace. These surfaces help to absorb warmth during peak daylight hours and then re-emit heat in the evening. Just as importantly, the presence of stone and gravel can accelerate the evaporation of dew and rain, keeping foliage dry and reducing the incidence of fungal leaf spot.

According to recent reports, taking a methodical approach at planting time helps your young lavender transition happily from nursery pot to garden dwelling. You need to set the correct root depth, establish good drainage, and avoid burying the woody crown. Do all this, and you can eliminate the risk of shock. Follow these steps to set your lavender up for vigorous, drought-resistant growth:.

Lavender is the ultimate low-maintenance perennial, provided you don't smother it with affection. If your usual gardening instinct involves wandering around with a watering can and tucking plants into cozy damp bark, you can relax. Lavender doesn’t want royal treatment. Think of ongoing care as gentle stewardship based on its Mediterranean temperament. Give it baking sun, dry roots, and an occasional appreciative nod, and it will reward you with months of fragrant abundance.

According to recent reports, during their first 6-8 weeks in the ground, young plants require consistent hydration. Provide a deep soaking once a week when the top 2 inches (5cm) of soil dry out. Once established, lavender is fiercely drought-tolerant. Mature English cultivars (L. angustifolia) and vigorous hybrid lavandins (L. × intermedia) thrive for weeks on natural rainfall alone and need supplemental water only during extended droughts. Spanish varieties might need an occasional sip when the dog days hit, but that’s it.

Always apply water directly to the base using a narrow-spout watering can. Something like the Yowon Long Spout Gold Watering Can from Amazon can help you deliver water straight to the root zone. Avoid overhead watering, which can trigger leaf spot. Of course, terracotta container-grown specimens dry out faster than bed-planted shrubs, so just check weekly during peak summer heat.

Lavender is naturally adapted to lean soils formed over weathered limestone, so its nutritional requirements are low. In fact, over-fertilizing is one of the quickest ways to ruin an established plant. Heavy applications of nitrogen-rich feeds trigger sappy growth at the expense of floral buds, and can also reduce the concentration of fragrant linalool and camphor oils that give lavender its signature aroma.

Instead of routine feeding, rely on soil conditioning. If your soil is nutrient-depleted, top-dress in early spring with an ultra-thin layer of well-aged organic compost or a light scattering of bone meal and greensand. You can buy Down to Earth Bone Meal from Walmart for a slow-release treat. In containers, a half-strength seaweed feed is also fine once a season. While French hybrid lavandins can handle a whisper of nutrition in spring, though, classic English varieties prefer to stay lean.

Recent findings suggest that spreading shredded hardwood, bark nuggets, or damp leaf mold around the base of lavender is a mistake. Organic wood mulches retain excessive moisture, slow evaporation, and harbor fungal spores. Furthermore, dark, damp bark cools the soil surface. The secret to proper lavender mulching lies in crunchy mineral alternatives. Crushed limestone is a favorite for English varieties, as it slowly releases calcium into the soil. Spanish cultivars love granite grit for keeping crowns high and dry.

Add a crisp, two-inch (5cm) layer of light-colored pea gravel, crushed limestone, or even crushed oyster seashells across the planting bed. Gravel does not rot and lets rainwater drain rapidly. Pale stones act like sun reflectors, bouncing daylight right up into the underbelly of the plant. You can buy Rain Forest White Pea Gravel from The Home Depot for a reflective base that reflects sunlight back up into the foliage.

According to recent reports, transplanting established lavender is challenging. This is because lavender forms a deep, brittle root network that resents disturbance. Older, woody plants rarely survive being moved, as severed roots struggle to regenerate in heavy soils. If relocation is essential, attempt only in early spring, just as fresh growth begins to show. Never transplant in midsummer or the damp cold of late fall.

To transplant lavender, prepare the new planting hole with coarse grit and lime. Dig wide and deep around the lavender to carry as much of the root along as you can. Once settled into its new home, give the top branches a trim, cutting back the soft green growth by about a third. This takes the pressure off the roots while they settle in and helps to reduce the risk of moisture stress.

Recent findings suggest that pruning is important if you want to keep your lavender in good shape. Doing this at least once a year helps to prevent splayed dead centers, and encourages flower production (and better fragrance!). However, there is one non-negotiable: never cut back into the old bare wood. Unlike deciduous shrubs, mature lavender wood is not likely to regenerate. Shearing into the gnarled brown center often results in permanent branch dieback or the loss of the entire shrub.

There are two seasonal stages. In early spring, once the first leaf shoots emerge from the lower stems, conduct a light wake-up trim. Snip away frost-damaged tips and gently shape the edges, taking care not to prune too early while hard freezes still threaten. Then in summer, after the main flowering ends, it’s time for the main structural cut. Using sharp bypass shears, clip away all spent flowers and remove one-third of the current season's soft green growth to form a smooth, rounded dome. This dome will help to shed any winter snow and also encourages dense branching.

Tailor your approach to your variety’s personality. Big French lavandins can take a confident, thorough haircut to tame wild wands, while compact English types prefer a gentle, elegant shaping. If you’re growing Spanish lavender with its rabbit-ear blooms, simply snip spent flower heads through spring to keep blooms coming. If you need a good snipping tool, you can buy Spear & Jackson CuttingSet8 Traditional Bypass & Anvil Secateur Set from Amazon. Just tuck the shears away before fall chills roll in.

Grow the right cultivar in the right place, and you can enjoy decades-long beauty. Breeders have refined lavender to excel in specific roles, from compact edging to storm-resistant mounds. These 5 standouts deliver exceptional performance, pest resistance, and exquisite blooms:.

There’s no getting around the fact that lavender success will depend on where you live. In the high heat and summer humidity of the Southeastern US and Gulf Coast, fungal melt is the biggest matter. Overcome this by planting in raised beds, doubling planting distances to 4 feet (1.2m) for better airflow, and choosing humidity-tolerant French hybrids (like Phenomenal or Sensational) rather than traditional English types.

It has been revealed that in severe northern zones (zones 4-5), deep winter freezes and dry winds can cause severe dieback. In these areas, stick to true English cultivars (Munstead or Hidcote), which tolerate sub-zero temperatures. Keep shrubs in well-drained soil on sheltered slopes where snow can form a natural blanket. And avoid late-season fertilization as this delays dormancy.

Sources indicate that in the sun-drenched, alkaline West and Southwest (zones 8-10), native conditions closely mirror the Mediterranean. Spanish lavenders and French toothed types thrive in lean native soils. The primary danger here is over-irrigation from lawn sprinklers. So just be sensible about your watering.

According to recent reports, growing lavender in pots is a dream, as long as you are thoughtful about drainage and watering. Containers are certainly an excellent workaround if you have heavy clay or damp native soil. However, stick to thick-walled, unglazed terracotta or breathable stone composite. Unglazed clay is naturally porous, allowing excess moisture to evaporate through the walls and ensuring critical root respiration.

Industry observers note that make sure your pot has a generous drainage hole. It’s also a good idea to elevate pots onto pot feet or risers to prevent drainage outlets sealing flat against patio stones. You can get Doggy Plant Pot Feet from Amazon to elevate heavy planters an inch off patio surfaces, guaranteeing free drainage flow and preventing trapped moisture.

For the potting blend, you need a super-gritty cocktail. Mix seven parts light potting compost with three parts chunky perlite or volcanic pumice. Never use potting mixes containing synthetic gel crystals. While bed-grown lavender rarely needs water once established, container roots dry rapidly. Water deeply only when the top 2 inches (5cm) is bone dry. Rotate each pot in your lavender container garden a quarter-turn every week, so plants receive balanced light for the liveliest, bee-friendly results.

It has been revealed that the best winter survival for lavender isn’t about fighting freezing temperatures, but preventing excess slush. This hinges on shielding lavender from standing wet and gales. In beds, cold-hardy English varieties and vigorous lavandins tolerate sub-zero temperatures down to zone 5. Just keep the root crown clear of soggy leaf debris, and erect a burlap windbreak in exposed northern sites.

Potted specimens are more vulnerable. In zone 6 and colder, move containers into an unheated garage, shed, or sheltered cold frame once nighttime temperatures consistently drop below 30°F (-1°C). Give them just a small cup of water once a month. Use Bloem Plant Caddies from The Home Depot to help wheel heavier containers inside.

If you're growing Spanish varieties, bring them indoors to a bright, cool windowsill before hard freezes arrive. Once the spring sun warms the patio and frost warnings disappear, ease pots back outdoors, hardening them off gradually in dappled shade.

It has been revealed that propagating lavender from stem cuttings is far more reliable than starting from seed, and the results of growing from lavender cuttings can be enormously satisfying. Lavender seed can be erratic, with low germination rates, and hybrid lavandins produce sterile seed that will not come true to type. Taking cuttings ensures a clone that preserves your parent’s exact flower color, growth habit and essential oil profile. You just need to be selective about timing and plant age.

In a recent development, the best time for taking lavender cuttings is mid-summer to early fall, using semi-ripe wood. These are stems of the current season’s growth that are firm and woody at the base but still green at the tip. Select healthy non-flowering shoots from vigorous, 2-4-year-old plants. Strip the foliage from the lower 2 inches (5cm) of a 3-4-inch stem, gently scraping a sliver of outer bark at the base. Dip the cut tip in rooting hormone and insert it into a sharp 50/50 mix of coarse horticultural sand and perlite.

Optionally, you can pop a clear plastic bag over the pot like a mini greenhouse. Then maintain bright, indirect light and gentle bottom warmth, keeping the rooting medium just barely damp. Roots normally develop in 4-6 weeks, which you can tell if you feel a resistance when you gently tug the cutting. Overwinter the young starts in a frost-free frame, planting them out into sunny borders in spring.

One of the best things about lavender’s scent is that it is a natural deterrent for most garden pests and troublemakers, including deer and rabbits. When lavender does encounter problems, it usually stems from environmental imbalances like stagnant airflow and heavy soils. Here are some of the main complications your plant might face:.

Industry observers note that lavender is naturally woody and develops hard, bare interior branches as it ages. This usually happens due to skipped annual pruning or improper shearing. Over time, outer branches get heavy, exposing the leafless core. While you cannot cut back into bare old wood to rejuvenate it, you can prevent it getting more pronounced. Prune annually in late summer by removing one-third of the soft green growth.

Unlike herbaceous perennials such as hostas or coneflowers, lavender is a true woody bush. All fresh growth must regenerate from active leaf nodes along the soft upper stems. If you cut beneath the lowest leafy nodes into the bare brown wood, the branch cannot recover. Always leave at least 2-3 inches (5-8cm) of green foliage intact when you’re trimming back.

Industry observers note that harvest on a warm, dry morning, once dew has evaporated. Ideally, cut stems when the bottom third of the florets have opened, but before the upper buds burst. At this stage, the concentration of essential oils is at its peak. Secure the cut stems in loose bundles with bands or twine for good air movement. Hang upside down in a dark, dry, airy space for 2-3 weeks. Keeping them out of direct sunlight locks in color.

Standard English varieties struggle with intense southern humidity and wet soils. High atmospheric moisture traps dampness against foliage, inviting fungal rot. If you garden in the south, plant in sharply draining raised beds or rock gardens amended with coarse grit. Better yet, choose humidity-tolerant French hybrids like Phenomenal or Sensational, bred to hold its own in sweltering southern summer heat.

In a recent development, life is sweeter with a little lavender in it. Whether you want to carve out a sun-baked border for a cloud of bumbles, frame your walkway with a billowing fragrant hedge, or cultivate a terracotta pot of blooms on a balcony, lavender elevates every space as surely as it plays with the senses. So come on, expand your purple horizons, and get ready to fall head over heels with a lifelong cottage garden icon….

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, nothing creates a cozy Christmas atmosphere quite like a home filled with beautiful seasonal aromas – but instead of reaching for scented candles, air fresheners or potpourri, why not let living plants provide a naturally wonderful fragrance? The holidays are rich with aromas from pine-scented garlands to pumpkin pies baking in the oven, and using Christmas plants to bring another layer of perfume makes your home feel even more warm and inviting.

While Christmas cactus, amaryllis and poinsettia top the lists of holiday houseplants for their fabulous flowers, there are plenty of plants that deserve a spot in your home for their fragrance, too. Alongside attractive greenery and beautiful blooms, these scented selections will add to the festive ambience.

Think beyond the usual seasonal smells of pine or warming spices and use these seasonal houseplants to enjoy sweet, fresh, floral, woodsy and even chocolatey aromas to scent your home this year.

Industry observers note that for a traditional Christmas fragrance with unique notes, rosemary (Salvia rosmarinus) should be a staple for the holidays. This woody perennial herb is evergreen and has a piney aroma mixed with citrus, floral and mint notes that works so well with more traditional holiday scents. You could trim your potted rosemary like a topiary into a Christmas tree profile, or leave it in its natural bushy shape and pluck stems to tuck among roast potatoes or plunge into holiday cocktails.

While traditional rosemary is fabulous just as it is, other varieties can offer more in the way of holiday decor and still be used in the kitchen. Tuscan Blue rosemary, available from trees.com, has the same pleasing scent with particularly glossy leaves (and highly ornamental blue blooms in spring and summer). Arp rosemary, available from Burpee, has the strongest fragrance of all and while it's capable of growing into a significant plant outside, it's easy to keep small in a pot.

In a recent development, provide a potted rosemary with bright light, ideally from a south-facing window, and potting soil that drains very well. Rosemary naturally grows in warm, dry climates but indoors it prefers cooler temperatures and a little more moisture, so just let the top inch of soil dry between waterings. This is a tough, adaptable plant so it can be grown outside year-round in zones 8-10, or simply pop it outdoors for spring and summer in colder zones.

Forcing bulbs indoors is a fun holiday project and paperwhites (Narcissus papyraceus) are among the easiest to grow. The delicate white blooms resemble daffodils and grow elegantly on tall stems, with a floral fragrance that complements other seasonal scents well. Grown in a decorative dish or bowl, paperwhites offer sophisticated décor and delicious perfume in one.

Industry observers note that unlike other bulbs, narcissus don’t require a chill period so there's still time to get holiday blooms if you hurry, as it only takes three to six weeks to force paperwhite bulbs. A good bet are Ziva paperwhite bulbs, available from Eden Brothers, as they're effortlessly elegant and the easiest to grow. For a little more frill, Erlicheer paperwhite bulbs, also available from Eden Brothers, enjoy the same appealing fragrance and even more petals.

Recent findings suggest that use shallow containers with potting mix or glass dishes with decorative gravel, which allows you to see the bulbs and some of the roots as they grow. In zones 9-11, paperwhites can be replanted outdoors once they've finished flowering.

For a floral perfume that carries the promise of spring, forced hyacinth bulbs are a must for the holidays. Hyacinths (Hyacinthus orientalis) smell intensely floral with notes of green growth, sweet honey and wholesome earthiness. As with paperwhites, you can grow these bulbs in containers with soil or use decorative glass containers to show off their interesting roots.

Bulbs need to be chilled for 10 to 14 weeks, then blooms takes three to four weeks to grow, so you'll need to buy pre-planted holiday hyacinths for flowers this year, which you'll find at some grocery stores as well as garden centers. But pop a note into your phone calendar now to remind yourself to plant hyacinth bulbs in September for bowls of fragrant Christmas flowers.

Once they bloom, keep your hyacinths in a cool spot to preserve the flowers for as long as possible. After flowering, you can replant bulbs outside in zones 4-8.

Cupressus macrocarpa ‘Goldcrest’ is a variety of lemon cypress in a unique shade of yellow-green with a delicious citrus aroma. If you feel that holiday scents are sometimes a little too sweet and cloying, this is the plant you need to balance that with a fresh, clean perfume. As this evergreen is Christmas tree-shaped, lemon cypress adds a new element to traditional holiday greenery too.

It has been revealed that A great option for growing in a pot is the dwarf lemon cypress 'Wilma Goldcrest', available from trees.com. Though capable of eventually growing to 6 feet high and 1-2 feet wide, by growing this compact form in a planter, you can easily keep it small enough to bring indoors as a holiday houseplant for many years to come.

Recent findings suggest that position lemon cypress where the foliage will be brushed against as this is how the aroma is released, or you can simply crush the foliage between finger and thumb for a fresh burst of fragrance whenever you fancy. Your lemon cypress will need bright light but fairly cool temperatures. Water the pot regularly to avoid total dryness, but don’t let the roots sit in soggy soil. This compact tree grows best outdoors so move it outside after the holidays in zones 7-11, or overwinter indoors as a houseplant in zones 3-6.

Scented geraniums (Pelargonium spp.) offer the ultimate opportunity to customize your holiday fragrance profile. There are varieties with foliage that smells like roses, citrus, apple, ginger, cinnamon, chocolate mint and even nutmeg. Mix and match or pair with other houseplants to concoct a signature Christmas scent.

Industry observers note that at this time of the year, the best place to find plants is via the Etsy scented geranium live plants hub which lists available stock from verified independent nurseries. You’ll get the most out of your scented geraniums by placing them where you can rub the leaves to release a burst of fragrance. They need a sunny spot, too, as well as soil that drains well. Water when the soil begins to dry and pinch back stems to keep the foliage dense.

Scented geraniums can be grown outdoors year-round in zones 10-11, while in cooler climates they're best treated as winter houseplants that enjoy the summer outside on a sunny patio.

It has been revealed that for a unique chocolatey aroma, Oncidium Heaven Scent 'Redolence' is an orchid with a wonderfully sweet chocolate fragrance. You’ll also enjoy the elegant spikes of burgundy and white flowers that last for a month or more. Look out, too, for Oncidium Aka Baby 'Raspberry Chocolate' with a lighter but no less lovely chocolate perfume.

It's best to buy speciality orchids from specialist nurseries, and to be sure you’ll have aromatic flowers for the holidays, buy a plant that is already in bud or bloom. Akatsuka Orchid Gardens is one such nursery, based in Hawaii and stocking both the Heaven Scent 'Redolence' orchid and 'Raspberry Chocolate' orchid in bud and bloom. These orchids grow best in bright but indirect light and in a potting mix designed specifically for orchids. Water when the mix is dry and avoid overwatering or letting the mix get soggy. Good air circulation is also a must, and keep orchids as houseplants year-round.

Recent findings suggest that when my boss passed away, I took in his older Red Heeler, Bob, so he didnât end up in the pound. I've been giving him turkey tail for his lumps, and he is overweight.

Industry observers note that itâs hard to walk him when it's 100 degrees out. For the last couple of months, he has been drinking so much water and urinating way more than usual. He mostly stays inside, and when I take him out to pee, the first thing when he comes back in is head for the water bowl, like he wants to replace what he just got rid of!

Any suggestions on what I could try?â.

It has been revealed that you have done something very kind by giving Bob a home after losing his person. It sounds like he is a senior boy who has already been through a lot, and it is wonderful that he has someone looking out for him. The increased drinking and urination you are seeing, especially since this has been going on for a couple of months, is something I would have checked rather than assuming it is just his age or the hot weather. Older dogs can develop several conditions that cause this combination of signs, including diabetes, kidney disease, and Cushing's disease.

I would schedule a veterinary examination and ask for some basic lab work, particularly blood tests and urinalysis. These can give us information that we simply cannot get from looking at Bob. Bloodwork can tell us about his blood glucose, kidney and liver function, electrolytes, and other changes that may help identify what is going on. A urine sample is just as valuable. It can show whether his kidneys are concentrating the urine properly, and can also detect glucose, ketones, protein, blood, inflammation, and other abnormalities. Depending on those results, his veterinarian may recommend some additional tests.

Industry observers note that please do not limit his water, even if it seems like he is drinking right back what he just urinated. In many of these conditions, the excessive thirst is the body's way of trying to replace fluid that is being lost. Taking water away can actually make him dehydrated and much sicker. Keep fresh water available at all times, and because of the heat, try to take him out during the cooler parts of the day. If you can, measuring approximately how much water he drinks in 24 hours would also be very helpful information for his veterinarian.

I would also recommend that he has the lumps properly checked rather than relying on turkey tail or other supplements. Some lumps are harmless, but others can be more serious, and we cannot tell the difference just by feeling or looking at them. A fine needle aspiration can often collect cells from a lump with very little discomfort and may give the veterinarian a much better idea of what it is. With Bob being overweight and having difficulty walking in the heat, getting his medical issues sorted out first will also make it much safer to work on his weight and mobility.

He has clearly found someone who cares about him, and sometimes the most loving thing we can do for an older dog is simply to find out what his body is trying to tell us.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that once you’ve cleaned out your summer containers, you might think it’s best to tip the remaining potting mix into the waste.
  • In a recent development, over the growing season, that potting soil loses some nutrients because plants take them up and water washes them away.
  • Recent findings suggest that some plants actually prefer leaner soil.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that once you’ve cleaned out your summer containers, you might think it’s best to tip the remaining potting mix into the waste. Don’t be too hasty. That mix could still have plenty of life left in it.

In a recent development, over the growing season, that potting soil loses some nutrients because plants take them up and water washes them away. Bulky materials, like peat moss and compost, break down over the summer, too. However, reusing potting soil is possible as long as the previous residents didn’t have diseases or serious pest infestations.

Recent findings suggest that some plants actually prefer leaner soil. Here, I describe six plants that are capable of thriving in old potting mix. I also provide some tips for refreshing the soil to give the new plants a little boost.

According to recent reports, nasturtium (Tropaeolum majus) is a beautiful flowering plant that grows as an annual in most gardens. Many types trail or vine, making them ideal for containers. The brilliant flowers come in shades of red, yellow, and orange, like in these Jewel Blend nasturtium seeds from Seed Needs on Amazon, which also offers other beautiful color mixes. Both the flowers and leaves are edible. If you live in USDA zone 9 or warmer, you can grow nasturtiums as perennials.

It has been revealed that nasturtiums are good candidates for recycled potting mix because they are unfussy, easy to grow, and generally thrive in poor soil. They are also easy to grow from seed. Sow seeds in your used potting mix next year when it’s warm enough. Place the container in a sunny spot and water when the top inch of soil dries.

Sources indicate that moss rose (Portulaca grandiflora) is another annual in most gardens. This low-growing succulent, native to South America, blooms in summer and fall with flowers that resemble small roses. You can find a lovely selection of moss rose seed varieties at Eden Brothers, with a choice of colors to brighten up your containers. Moss rose thrives in poor, rocky, or sandy soil, making it ideal for containers. Plants need good drainage, so they can sometimes struggle in beds with heavy soil or poor drainage.

In a recent development, grow your moss roses in reused potting mix enhanced with perlite, like this Riare organic perlite on Amazon, or something similar to boost drainage. Place them in a full-sun spot and let the soil dry out in between waterings. Avoid overfertilizing, which can lead to more leaves and fewer flowers.

Sedums (Sedum spp.) are reliable and popular perennials for garden beds, but they also grow well in containers. This is a large group of plants, many of which are succulents suited to dry, poor soil. Many gardeners love stonecrops like ‘Autumn Joy,’ which turn gorgeous shades of deep red in fall. You can buy Autumn Joy sedum from Nature Hills to enjoy its colorful late-season display. You can also choose from among low-growing and taller clump-forming sedums.

In a recent development, the most crucial part of refreshing old soil for growing sedum is to add a material, like perlite, to improve drainage. Place your pots in a sunny location and water only when the soil dries. Avoid using too much, if any, fertilizer.

In a recent development, hens and chicks (Sempervivum spp.) are diminutive succulents that grow in rosettes and have delightfully fleshy leaves that can be bluish-green, copper, gold, reddish, or even two-toned. You can enjoy a mix of varieties with this hens and chicks plant collection from Hirt's Gardens Store on Amazon. While hens and chicks flower, they are grown mostly for their attractive foliage. Hardy perennials in many growing regions, hens and chicks also make great container plants. They produce small offsets, the chicks, that can be repotted for propagation.

Hens and chicks naturally grow in poor, rocky soil, so they should do well in your spent potting mix. Just be sure to add additional material to boost drainage. The best containers for hens and chicks are shallow and have adequate drainage holes, like this Deroma clay bowl planter from Target. Grow them in full sun or very light shade and water sparingly, letting the potting mix dry between waterings.

Calendula (Calendula officinalis), also known as pot marigold, is a short-lived perennial in zones 9 through 11, and an annual elsewhere. Though it is considered a flowering herb, many people grow calendula solely for its ornamental value. The flowers are daisy-like and usually bright orange or yellow, although they can also be red, white, or pink. You can pick up calendula seeds cheaply on Amazon, but Eden Brothers offers some gorgeous varieties, including the Pacific Beauty Mix and the Sunset Buff calendula pictured here.

Industry observers note that A Mediterranean native, calendula appreciates warmth, sunlight, and well-draining soil. It won’t tolerate soggy soil. It can thrive in poor soil but benefits from a little refresh of old potting mix with compost. Water your potted calendula regularly, but don’t let the soil get waterlogged. Deadhead the flowers throughout the season to encourage additional blooms.

Like calendula, cosmos (Cosmos bipinnatus) are mostly grown as annuals and are only hardy in zones 9 and higher. Cosmos are easy to grow from seed and reward you with feathery foliage and delicate flowers in shades of red, pink, white, yellow, and orange. Burpee sells a wide variety of cosmos seeds, including the beautiful ‘Sensation Mix’ pictured here. They make great cut flowers.

While cosmos tolerate poor soil, it’s best to refresh the old potting mix a little. Then, you can sow seeds and place the pot in a location with full sun. Use a large container, as cosmos can grow quite tall. Water the seeds and seedlings regularly to keep the soil moist, and then only sparingly.

Sources indicate that while all of these, and many other plants, tolerate leaner soil, all plants will appreciate a little refresh of old, tired soil. A few simple steps will give you better results over the course of the growing season:.

Remember that not all old soil should be used. Disease and pests can be passed on, so don’t take the risk. Also, if you’re growing plants that aren’t as tough as those listed here, it’s best to start over with fresh potting mix. You should also replace the mix if it has broken down so much that it becomes muddy and dense when wet.

It has been revealed that remember, old potting soil doesn’t necessarily belong in the trash. With a little refreshing and by choosing the right plants, you can recycle that old mix and use it for at least one more year.

What if your senior dog could help scientists learn more about how dogs age, and potentially help future generations of dogs live healthier lives?

According to recent reports, that is the opportunity behind a major clinical trial from the Dog Aging Project, a research collaboration focused on giving us a better understanding of canine aging. The project is right now looking for older, healthy dogs to participate in the Test of Rapamycin in Aging Dogs, better known as TRIAD.

This study is attracting renewed attention following a recent 60 Minutes report on the Dog Aging Project and its work investigating why dogs age the way they do and how their golden years might be made healthier.

In a recent development, TRIAD is not simply asking how long dogs can live. Researchers are trying to understand if a medication called rapamycin can influence the aging process and improve health in older dogs.

Sources indicate that rapamycin, also known as sirolimus or Rapamune, is a macrolide drug with immunosuppressive and antitumor properties. This medication has been used in human medicine for more than two decades, including in patients who have undergone kidney transplantation.

The interest in rapamycin and aging comes from a different area of research. Studies in laboratory organisms found that rapamycin can extend lifespan in several species, including mice, yeast, worms, and flies. Now, researchers want to find out whether those benefits could extend to our pets.

The Dog Aging Projectâs TRIAD trial is a multicenter study involving researchers and veterinary hospitals at universities across the United States, including Tufts University. The TRIAD trial is investigating whether rapamycin can influence lifespan and, importantly, promote healthy aging in companion dogs.

For veterinary science, one of the most interesting parts of aging research is the difference between lifespan and healthspan.

Recent findings suggest that lifespan is how long an animal lives. Healthspan is the portion of that life spent in good health.

Living longer is great, but what matters just as much is how dogs feel during those extra years. More time with the family means less if a dog is struggling with chronic illness, having trouble getting around, or experiencing cognitive decline. The goal isn't just to add years to a dog's life. It's to help them enjoy more of those years feeling good.

TRIAD is examining several areas of canine health, including cognitive function, heart function, immunity, and cancer incidence.

Be able to cooperate with examinations, including blood collection and cardiac ultrasound, without sedation.

Have normal diagnostic findings at enrollment.

Clinical trial sites are located throughout the United States.

Researchers will follow the dogs for another two years to see how they age and whether any differences emerge over time. In total, owners will bring their dogs to a clinical trial site seven times during the three-year study.

There's also a practical advantage. Dogs age much faster than humans. This allows researchers to track changes in their health over a few years instead of waiting decades. That's a major deal when you're trying to understand what happens as the body ages.

But this isn't just about what dogs can teach us about ourselves. What researchers discover will help dogs, too.

In a recent development, aging isn't a single disease that can be treated with one medication. Maybe getting up becomes harder, walks get shorter, or a dog who's always been sharp seems a little confused. Sometimes these changes happen gradually, and it's easy to chalk them up to old age.

The more we learn about what's actually happening in an aging dog's body, the better chance veterinarians have of spotting problems earlier and finding ways to help dogs feel good for as long as possible.

The project explains that dogs who do not qualify for TRIAD can still make a meaningful contribution to understanding canine aging.

The more variety researchers can study, the better picture they can get of why some dogs stay healthy well into their senior years while others develop health problems earlier.

Industry observers note that when it comes to canine aging, the goal isn't just to help dogs live longer. It's to help them feel good for more of those years, stay active, and keep enjoying life with their families.

Apparently, Cats Are Good for the National Mood.

The researchers found a positive correlation between estimated cat density and national happiness scores. In plain English, countries with more cats tended to report higher happiness levels.

Interesting? Absolutely. Proof that cats make people happier? Not quite.

In a recent development, the study compared data from entire countries rather than following individuals before and after they adopted a cat. So it cannot tell whether cats improve happiness, happier people are more likely to keep cats, or something else is going on.

We know that pet cats offer companionship and amazing moments of genuine connection. In a recent development, but personal experience and national statistics are two different things. A purring companion can brighten someone's day; proving that cats raise an entire country's happiness score takes considerably more evidence.

It has been revealed that hereâs where the story gets interesting. Not too surprisingly, economic prosperity had a stronger relationship with happiness than cat density. The relationship between national income and happiness had a Pearson correlation coefficient of around 0.80, compared with 0.62 for cat numbers.

In other words, a country's wealth was more closely associated with how happy its people reported feeling than the estimated number of cats living there. Money certainly doesn't guarantee happiness, but it can definitely make life less stressful when we compare it with living with no resources.

Industry observers note that financial security can help afford nutritious food, veterinary visits, pay the rent, and have the peace of mind of being able to cover unexpected medical bills. Access to healthcare, personal safety, and stable living conditions are important too.

Recent findings suggest that this wider picture could help explain why cat density and happiness move together. The relationship might reflect the broader social environment rather than some magical feline effect.

Cats can enrich our lives, absolutely. But even the most accomplished biscuit-maker cannot fix unaffordable housing. And a cat's approach to financial planning remains questionable at best. Knocking an expensive object off a shelf to demand dinner is hardly a sustainable economic strategy.

The researchers also examined Toxoplasma gondii, a parasite that reproduces in cats and other felids.

To explore this, researchers considered two types of antibodies: one that can sometimes indicate a more recent infection and another generally associated with past exposure. Thereâs another crucial detail. The researchers used infection estimates from pregnant women, and that may not accurately represent the entire population.

Recent findings suggest that most importantly, the study does not prove that T. gondii causes unhappiness. Industry observers note that T. gondii can spread through undercooked contaminated meat, contaminated soil or produce, water, and accidental ingestion of infectious material from cat feces. Simply petting a cat or sharing a home with one does not automatically cause infection.

It has been revealed that pets can offer us comfort and companionship, but research on pet ownership and mental health has produced mixed results. Benefits vary between individuals, and caring for an animal can also bring financial pressure, stress, disrupted sleep, allergies, property loss or damage, and even grief.

It has been revealed that cats are not standardized wellness products with a purring function. Some adore cuddles; others prefer admiration from a respectable distance. The study points to a connection between cat density and national happiness, but it cannot prove that cats make countries happier or that toxoplasmosis explains national differences. The findings raise interesting questions; they don't settle the debate.

During pregnancy, having someone else clean the litter tray is recommended, but a healthy cat should not need to be rehomed because of toxoplasmosis concerns. Good hygiene is more useful than panic.

Ultimately, happiness depends on a complicated mix of economic security, health, social circumstances, and personal relationships. Cats may enrich human lives, but no single animal can explain the mood of an entire nation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanks to her stint in The Family Stone, Sarah Jessica Parker's name has long been synonymous with the holidays for fans – and even more so now she's shared her Christmas tree trick with us all!

Yes, it is now possible to give your Christmas tree that Carrie Bradshaw stamp of approval! And, somewhat gloriously, SJP's approach to festive decor has the same sort of wonderfully unfussy vibe as Michelle Obama's twig tree, which means you don't need a celebrity-sized budget to recreate the look. In fact, all you really need is baby's breath.

Sources indicate that this underrated flower has spent most of its life being a supporting actor to bigger and better roses, or a wispy filler flower tucked into grocery store bouquets. But when Kristin Davis posted an Instagram video of herself arranging flowers blindfolded (as one does), Sarah Jessica Parker left a surprising comment: “You can use babies breath in your Christmas tree.” Say what?

Now, Kristin Davis (who worked at a florist in college) wasn’t keen on using it for her own tree (very Charlotte-coded), but she did share a rule worth stealing: if you're going to do it, then always arrange flowers in odd numbers, like three or five.

In a recent development, for me, though, SJP’s comment about using baby’s breath in her Christmas tree has set my imagination alight! And with that in mind, I asked some experts how I could use them in my own holiday decoration this year.

In a recent development, the biggest risk when it comes to stealing Sarah Jessica Parker's idea is overdoing it. Roberta Sabbatini, founder of ItalianTouch Events, says, “The main mistake is using too much. The beauty of baby’s breath is its lightness.” Morgan Brooks of Plant Style Home puts it even better, saying, “One loose spiral is elegant. Three is a snowstorm, and the tree disappears behind it.”.

Remember that odd-number rule? CEO of Florals Memories Nadi Melam clips her baby’s breath into “clouds” and adds them in threes, noting, “Baby’s breath looks beautiful on trees because of negative space.” Translation: let the tree breathe!

Industry observers note that for a spiral, Brooks gathers five to seven stems, wires each bunch at the base, and tucks the ends deep into the branches. Sabbatini also skips pushing loose stems into the tree and instead secures each little bundle with florist wire or ribbon.

Recent findings suggest that fresh baby’s breath is a diva out of water. Brooks says fresh stems “wilt within a day or two indoors,” while dried versions keep their shape all season and can be packed away for next year. Melam agrees that dried is “far easier to work with.” If you do love fresh, just be sure to add it on Christmas Eve.

If you don't have time for the drying process, this Bexikou dried baby’s breath bouquet comes ready to use, and its short white stems are well suited to wiring into small, airy clusters for your tree.

Drying your own for a Sarah Jessica Parker-style tree is simple. Bundle five to seven stems with twine, hang them upside down in a dark, warm, well-ventilated room, and check after five days, as outlined in our guide to growing baby’s breath. If you’re short on time, ready-dried bunches work just as well.

On an artificial tree, Brooks adds fine floral wire around the branch wire, since the stems are too light to stay put when someone brushes past.

Sources indicate that warm white lights, clear glass ornaments, and velvet ribbon are baby’s breath’s best friends. Brooks adds pearl baubles and silver or soft gold ribbon to the list, but warns that rustic burlap and heavy red ornaments “fight it.” Treat baby’s breath as one of just two or three ideas on the tree, not the whole script.

Pair your baby’s breath with a strand of Northlight 100-count warm white LED mini lights, which stay cool to the touch and give the soft, candlelit glow that suits a delicate white filler.

Dried stems are brittle and, as Melam notes, highly flammable. Use cool LED lights and keep bunches away from hot bulbs and open flames. Baby’s breath is also mildly toxic to cats, so if pets are around, keep it to the upper two-thirds of the tree and sweep up anything that falls.

Recent findings suggest that baby’s breath is easy to grow, so sow seeds next spring, cut and dry the blooms in summer, and next December’s tree is sorted. Will your tree look like a Manhattan brownstone from a certain Sarah Jessica Parker-fronted TV series? Possibly, but only if you resist the urge to add a fourth bunch.

Industry observers note that A female cat suddenly raising her hindquarters into the air, her tail swishing suggestively, can seem like a strange new behavior. In an unspayed female, though, it's often one of the clearest signs that she's gone into heat.

Heat, more correctly called âestrusâ, is a normal part of a cat's reproductive cycle, but it can bring several noticeable changes in behavior. Unspayed cats typically experience their first heat or season between six and nine months old, although some can start even earlier. After that first season, she will continue to come into heat roughly every 21 days, but during months with longer daylight hours, the cycle can repeat every two to three weeks.

It has been revealed that as âlong-dayâ breeders, the female reproductive cycle of cats tends to be linked to warmer seasons when daylight hours are longer. However, depending on the climate and location, they can continue to cycle throughout the year.

Knowing what to look for can make the sudden change in behavior much easier to understand.

The insistent and attention-grabbing raising of the butt is certainly one of the hallmarks of a cat in estrus, but, like with so many feline behaviors, context is key. Here are some classic signs that are commonly â but not exclusively â displayed by a cat in heat.

It has been revealed that the most recognizable behavior is the one that often gets the most attention. A female cat may raise her hindquarters and move her tail off to one side, a posture sometimes described as âpresentingâ.

This is a way for a female to signal to males that she's receptive to mating.

However, the posture by itself doesn't necessarily mean a cat is in heat, and many spayed females, and even male cats, will raise their hindquarters when being petted or while stretching their front legs. It's therefore more useful when considered alongside the other signs of heat.

A raised bum and attentive behavior from a spayed/neutered cat is often a sign of trust and affection.

In a recent development, A cat in heat can become considerably more vocal. The sounds can be loud and intense, and some owners may even mistake the vocalizing for a sign that their cat is in pain.

In a recent development, on its own, though, this behavior isn't usually cause for alarm in a cat that is otherwise showing the typical signs of heat. The vocalizing is part of the way a female calls for a mate.

Frequent vocalizing can have other causes, including illness or pain, so a cat showing additional signs that something isn't right should be checked by a vet.

Rolling around on the floor is hardly unusual for a cat. Cats of either sex may roll around while playing, seeking attention, or scratching an itch.

During heat, however, a female may do it more frequently as part of the behavioral changes that come with her reproductive cycle.

Like raising the hindquarters, rolling isn't enough to confirm that a cat is in heat on its own. It becomes more meaningful when it appears alongside several of the other signs.

In a recent development, some cats become noticeably more affectionate when they're in heat. They may seek out attention more often, stay close to their owners, or generally seem more interested in interaction than usual.

Recent findings suggest that there are plenty of other reasons a cat might become more affectionate. A cat could be looking for warmth in cold weather or seeking extra attention after being separated from an owner.

That makes increased affection more useful as part of a pattern rather than as a standalone sign.

In a recent development, urine spraying is more commonly associated with unneutered male cats, but did you know that females can spray too? During heat, the scent is thought to help attract potential mates.

Recent findings suggest that at the same time, urinating outside the litter box can have many other explanations. Litter box problems, behavioral concerns, and medical complications can all cause changes in bathroom habits.

If a cat starts consistently going outside the litter box, it's worth discussing with a vet rather than assuming the behavior is simply related to heat.

Industry observers note that A female cat in heat may become more determined to get outside. Scratching at doors or windows can be part of that behavior, particularly when a cat is trying to find a mate.

In a recent development, keeping her indoors is especially important during this period. An unspayed female that gets outside has a risk of becoming pregnant, as well as facing the usual dangers associated with roaming, including traffic, animal attacks, and getting lost.

Responsible pet ownership means spaying or neutering your cat. By removing the ovaries and uterus, spaying stops the reproductive cycle permanently, preventing unwanted litters, reducing the risk of uterine infections, and meaningfully lowering the risk of mammary cancer. It also reduces the risks of cats escaping, fighting, and being hit by a car.

There are no health or behavioral advantages to allowing your female cat to have a litter, so veterinary advice is to spay and neuter most cats by 6 months.

Until then, recognizing the signs of heat can make a sudden change in behavior much less confusing. A female cat raising her hindquarters, becoming unusually vocal, rolling around, seeking extra attention, spraying, or trying to get outside may simply be responding to a normal part of her reproductive cycle.

Of course, it may simply be a catâs way of signalling trust and affection!

Industry observers note that halloween candy can be dangerous for dogs, and the wrappers create an additional hazard. Certain ingredients in sweets, including chocolate and xylitol, can be toxic to dogs, while swallowed wrappers can cause choking or digestive problems.

Industry observers note that keeping candy in a closed container at home is a good starting point, but the risk doesn't end at the front door. Keeping a close eye on what a dog sniffs or picks up can help prevent an unwanted snack from turning into a veterinary emergency.

Costumes for dogs can be adorable and hilarious, but only if the dog agrees. Not every dog feels happy playing dress-up, so itâs important to pay attention to how they respond.

A costume should fit comfortably without restricting movement or creating opportunities for the dog to become tangled. An outfit that fit last year may now be too tight, while one bought for a puppy to grow into could be awkward or unsafe in the meantime.

Before heading out or welcoming visitors, check that the costume fits properly and your pup can walk comfortably in it.

Industry observers note that A Halloween costume can look adorable on a dog, but wearing one safely requires supervision. Some dogs become fascinated by their outfits and start chewing at loose fabric or accessories, potentially creating a choking hazard.

Industry observers note that there's no reason every dog has to avoid costumes, provided the outfit is comfortable and the dog tolerates wearing it. But if the dog needs to be left alone, take the costume off. It's a simple precaution that reduces the chance of an otherwise harmless outfit causing trouble.

Halloween can be overwhelming for dogs that struggle with noise, unfamiliar people, or constant activity. Trick-or-treaters arrive throughout the evening, and costumes can make even familiar surroundings feel different.

A dog that becomes overexcited or anxious may benefit from having somewhere quiet to retreat. A separate room with a comfortable bed, fresh water, and familiar toys can provide a welcome break from the commotion.

Make sure visitors understand that the dog shouldn't be disturbed if it chooses to settle somewhere away from the activity.

Jack-o'-lanterns, lights, and other Halloween decorations can make a home feel festive, but curious dogs may see them as things to investigate or chew. Keep decorations out of reach, particularly anything that could be harmful if swallowed.

Industry observers note that real candles inside pumpkins also pose a risk if a dog knocks one over. Battery-operated alternatives are a safer choice, especially in areas where pets can wander freely.

Glow sticks and glowing bracelets help make children more visible during evening trick-or-treating, but their bright colors and flexible shapes can also attract a dog's attention.

Sources indicate that the liquid inside can cause irritation and may be harmful if swallowed. A dog that bites through a glow stick could end up ingesting the contents, so these items should be kept well away from curious mouths.

Check the ground during walks, too, particularly on Halloween night when discarded glow sticks and bracelets may be lying around. If a dog chews or swallows one, contact a vet for advice.

Handing out candy can mean opening the front door dozens of times in a single evening. For a dog that's curious, excitable, or easily frightened, those repeated opportunities can make an escape more likely.

Closing the door between visitors helps prevent a dog from slipping outside unnoticed. Another option is to step outside to greet trick-or-treaters and close the door behind you.

Keeping the dog in a separate room during busy periods adds another layer of protection. It also reduces the chance of a dog becoming startled by costumed visitors appearing at the entrance.

An identification tag and microchip are always a good idea, but they become particularly notable on a night when doors are opening frequently, and unusual sights may startle a dog.

If a dog escapes, an ID tag with current contact details gives whoever finds it a straightforward way to get in touch. A microchip provides another means of identifying the dog and helping it return home.

Check that the dog's tag is attached securely and that the contact information associated with its microchip is up to date. These small steps can make a significant difference if a dog gets loose.

Sources indicate that halloween can be stressful and dangerous for dogs, but it doesnât have to be. Keeping candy secured, choosing comfortable costumes, providing a quiet retreat, and making sure the front door stays closed can prevent many of the problems associated with the holiday.

It's also worth remembering that dogs may react unpredictably to unfamiliar costumes and unusual activity, even if they're normally relaxed around visitors. Staying attentive from the first doorbell to the last helps keep the evening enjoyable for everyone, including the four-legged members of the household.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, there's something rather magical about spotting an owl in your backyard. These mysterious nighttime visitors can be surprisingly elusive, but there are ways to make your garden a more welcoming place for them. And no, you don't need acres of woodland or a sprawling country estate to get your very own owl hangout started.

The secret is to think beyond the owls themselves (although there's never any harm in making an owl nest box) and create a garden that supports the wildlife they depend on.

Whether you want to lure in your birth month owl, or find yourself – much like Justin Bieber – welcoming in any owl that flits by, there are plenty of ways to make your backyard more appealing to these beautiful birds of prey. And the good news? Well, you can make a surprisingly major difference with just five plants.

Sources indicate that that's right, folks! If you want more owls in your garden, that means providing shelter for small mammals, encouraging insects and other prey, and offering trees and shrubs where owls can perch, roost or potentially nest.

From tall native grasses to berry-producing shrubs and evergreen trees, then, these are some of the best additions for creating an owl-friendly backyard.

Switchgrass (Panicum virgatum) is a fantastic native grass for an owl-friendly garden, particularly if you have a sunny spot where you can let it grow relatively undisturbed.

In a recent development, why? Well, because its tall stems and dense clumps provide valuable cover for small mammals, including voles and mice, which are important prey for many owl species. The grass also offers shelter for other wildlife through winter, when more exposed parts of the garden can become less hospitable.

In a recent development, switchgrass is particularly useful in meadow-style plantings, where it can grow alongside native wildflowers. It produces attractive seedheads in late summer and fall, too, and it's a relatively low-maintenance perennial once established.

According to recent reports, give it a sunny position and well-drained soil, then, and leave some of its growth standing over winter rather than cutting everything back in fall. You may just find it swiftly becomes your newly introduced favorite garden plant, let alone the best part of your owl hangout!

It has been revealed that if you want to make your garden more appealing to owls, don't underestimate the value of evergreen trees! Native pines and spruces provide year-round cover, with dense branches offering potential daytime roosting spots and sheltered perches. Their evergreen foliage can also make wildlife feel more protected from disturbance and exposure.

Sources indicate that different owl species have different preferences, but trees are an notable part of the habitat for many woodland-dwellers like barred owls. Some species also use natural cavities in mature trees for nesting.

Recent findings suggest that if you have room, consider something like this stunning Eastern White Pine from Nature Hills. Just remember that a newly planted sapling is unlikely to become an instant owl retreat, though, so it's always better to preserve mature trees where you can!

Sources indicate that A slightly wild patch of blackberry brambles (Rubus spp.) might not be everyone's idea of a perfectly manicured garden, but it's a genius addition to anyone hoping to turn their yard into an owl hangout. After all, blackberry thickets provide dense cover for small critters and nesting birds, not to mention food and shelter for plenty others besides.

It has been revealed that why does this matter for owls? Because a garden that supports a healthy range of small animals can help provide the prey that visiting owls need, of course! And you don't have to let blackberries take over your entire yard, either. A small patch of something like Baby Cakes® Blackberry Bush from Nature Hills along a boundary or at the back of a wildlife-friendly border can provide plenty of habitat value.

Just remember that brambles can spread, so give them room and keep growth away from paths and areas where people regularly walk.

Serviceberry (Amelanchier spp.) is a beautiful native shrub or small tree that brings several seasons of wildlife interest to the garden; think white flowers that attract pollinators, followed by edible berries in summer, which are enjoyed by birds and other wildlife.

Its value doesn't stop with the berries; serviceberry also supports insects and provides useful woody cover, helping to create a more diverse backyard habitat. For an owl-friendly garden, this is all about supporting the wider food web... but hey, it helps that it's a stunner, too!

According to recent reports, goldenrod (Solidago spp.) is often overlooked as a wildlife plant, but its bright yellow flowers provide an important late-season source of nectar and pollen for bees, butterflies and other insects. Those insects, in turn, help support other wildlife, including small birds and mammals.

It has been revealed that some smaller owl species also eat large insects, making insect-rich habitats like goldenrod a must for your owl hangout! Especially as it's a lovely way to add late-summer and fall color to your garden. Many varieties are native to North America, and once established, they're generally easy to grow.

Something like the Fireworks Solidago (Goldenrod) Plant from Burpee is a great way to go!

These five plants are a great starting point for your owl hangout, but there are plenty of other native choices that can help make your backyard more wildlife-friendly. #.

Sources indicate that viburnums, for example, produce berries that feed birds and other wildlife, while their dense branching offers useful cover, too. Native dogwoods offer flowers, berries and dense branching that can provide shelter for wildlife, not to mention some much-added beauty to any yard (there's a reason they're swiftly replacing magnolias for a lot of people!).

Junipers offer dense year-round cover and provide berry-like cones that are eaten by birds and small mammals. And purple coneflowers (Echinacea purpurea) attract pollinators and produce seedheads that feed birds and other critters, too.

It has been revealed that of course, planting is a brilliant starting point, but there are a few other things you can do to make your garden more appealing to these fascinating birds. As ever, try leaving some areas of longer grass and natural vegetation rather than tidying every corner. Keep mature trees where possible, particularly those with natural cavities, and consider whether a species-appropriate owl nest box might be suitable for your local area.

According to recent reports, it's also important to avoid rodent poisons, as owls can be exposed to rodenticides when they eat poisoned mice and rats. Keep lights to a minimum after the sun goes down, as they can confuse nocturnal birds and critters. And, finally, remember that owls need peace and quiet; take care to avoid disturbing potential roosting and nesting areas, particularly during breeding season.

You might not spot an owl straight away, but by planting for wildlife and allowing your garden to become a little more natural, you'll be creating a much richer habitat for all sorts of visitors. And who knows? Before too long, your owl hangout might just be the most buzzing nightspot in town...

She previously served as digital editor at Stylist magazine, and has written extensively for Ideal Home, Woman & Home, Homes & Gardens, and a handful of other titles. Kayleigh is passionate about wildlife-friendly gardening, and recently cancelled her weekend prepares to build a mini pond when her toddler found a frog living in their water barrel. As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.

Letâs Be S.M.A.R.T. in Keratea, Greece, is a truly unique organization, presently home to over 100 cats and 13 dogs, living in a cage-free, home-like, villa-style environment. S.M.A.R.T. stands for Successfully Managing Animal Rights Today, and for Julie Kelley, founder and manager of this international animal welfare organization, that means working towards global animal welfare, sharing essential information and facts about animals worldwide, and helping people understand the benefits that come from treating animals with compassion and care.

I had been traveling to Greece since 1998 and would see the issues with stray cats and dogs. I felt very comfortable in Greece. I had business with Greek nationals in Fresh York, learned a lot of the language, and understood the cultural differences. I felt it was my mission to create Letâs Be S.M.A.R.T. to help people understand the great benefits animals provide to us humans and to educate young people as well. Of course, after a couple of years, it was hard not to take in the first kitty who gave birth, and well, it just grew exponentially from there! Since 2007, we have added many programs and special projects to continue our quest to provide the best we can for our strays.

Industry observers note that letâs be S.M.A.R.T. aims to educate the public about the importance of animals by raising awareness of their rights, well-being, and care. We believe in thinking globally and acting locally by supporting special projects as they arise and, through our programs, bringing communities together to promote responsible animal care.

According to recent reports, in Greece, our campaign is primarily centred on reducing the suffering, abuse, and neglect of animals while increasing public awareness of their needs and rights. These include running an innovative and modern foster home, managing a rehoming program for rescued animals, and collaborating with municipalities to implement effective stray animal care initiatives. We also provide practical solutions for supporting strays in urban communitiesâsuch as ensuring access to food and waterâand we actively engage philanthropic individuals who travel to Greece to volunteer, learn about shelter medicine, and receive training in best practices in animal care.

In a recent development, the creation of the sanctuary and setting up the organization in Greece was a huge accomplishment. Let's be S.M.A.R.T. is always evolving with fresh ideas to make life better for the cats and dogs we have in our care.

Recent findings suggest that our campaign model is unique in Greece. We have created the âSMART Starfish approachâ in which all five arms must function together to create the best outcome.

Each arm of the starfish represents a core pillar of our mission:.

Sterilization â controlling population growth at its source.

Medical Care & Microchipping â restoring health and identity.

Feeding & Shelter â stability, nourishment, and safety.

Education & Community â knowledge that shapes future behavior.

NGO Collaboration â collective strength through partnership.

For years, our programs and ideas have been influencing how animal charities operate and making permanent changes for a better future for animal welfare in Greece.

In a recent development, we created the following programs: Volunteer, SMART Family Video Series, Veterinary Internship, SMART Yards, and Adoption Vacation, all of which are operational every day and are detailed on the Programs page on our website, if you would like to take a closer look. We could not function without the help of our amazing Volunteers.

We successfully found wonderful homes for 73 cats in 2025. I'm not 100% sure, but I would say we are one of the leading cat adopters in Greece!

We receive multiple enquiries from tourists who have found a cat or kitten, and they want to take it home with them to their country. Many times they have cared for them during their stay, provided medicine, bottle-fed babies, etc. This has become increasingly common, with visitors seeing cats all over Greece. Therefore, I decided to offer the Adoption-Vacation as a package. We care for the kitten or cat until it is ready to travel, taking care of the necessary vaccines, passport, microchip, etc. Once the cat is ready to travel, we make travel arrangements with the adopter.

Recent findings suggest that you can see our cats, kittens, and dogs for adoption on our website and have a video chat with us about your requirements and meet a cat if you have already fallen in love (we created a Kitty Picker to help you choose the character of your cat), and then arrange a visit with us when you arrive in Greece. If the home check is secured, we arrange the papers for your new pet to travel home with you. Or we can foster a cat you rescue while you are in Greece and deal with the veterinary needs, papers etc. The cat can travel after you leave with a flight buddy or one of our volunteers.

What better souvenir to have from Greece than a beautiful cat that needed special love and care?

Everything we do is linked. The more sterilizations we achieve, the safer and healthier the animals are in the community; they are interacting better with each other, and people know they are sterilized.

Industry observers note that we would like the municipalities and communities all over Greece to enjoy the benefits of the SMART Yards and help take care of the animals. Working together is the future. We are also collaborating with some officials regarding some policies involving the strays and to help create some standards for housing the strays. Animals and people need to coexist in a humane way. Not every cat needs to be inside a home but can remain cared for and part of our ecosystem.

In a recent development, A rather massive goal is to find someone to help us purchase the property we rent, make refurbishments and sustainable features, and add a vet clinic for shared use with other charities and our vet interns. This is a tall order, but we are looking for someone who would like to leave a legacy.

We also want to extend our ability to provide food and shelter after sterilization so that every animal is cared for.

Our animals live in a home-style environment, so every day is the same as if they were living in a family home. Cats are either in bedrooms; we have a retirement room, a special dietary needs room, and a kitten nursery, each with cats that are selected to share a room together, or they are in the main house and free to mingle and hang out on our netted balconies in cute wooden houses and take in the fresh air and nature, since we are in a rural setting, just 15 minutes from Athens International Airport.

According to recent reports, some of the funniest moments are with kittens and playful cats. Plus, bonded pairs â we have a husband-and-wife team called Jasper and Margot who need to be adopted together, and they are very entertaining with their games and spats.

Sources indicate that cats and dogs choose who they like and want to go home with. We find people fall in love with cats that come to them, and a chemistry is formed. Sometimes a visitor leaves, and they cannot stop thinking about the cat they fell in love with and make an application to adopt. We are so happy when this happens. We have repeat adoptions from families and visitors all over the world. We also have Sponsors and Patreon for people to support our work.

Volunteering is open to everyone around the world who would like to come to stay and help us. If you love animals, it's an opportunity to help save lives. It's pure joy to see a cat or dog that was sick transform into good health and finally live in a wonderful family home. That's what the team at Let's be S.M.A.R.T. wants for them all: to be safe, healthy, and happy.

People can also help by following, subscribing, and sharing us on socials. Donations are greatly appreciated, as are supplies, and we created the Amazon Wishlist so gifts can be sent to us directly from Amazon Germany, tax-free.

It has been revealed that if youâre visiting Greece and see a lot of stray cats, itâs a good idea to ask around if there is a local organization helping to take care of them. If you see an injured cat, you should immediately try to find a responsible person or contact the local police.

You can also post on local social media groups to try to find help. Most of the cats we take into our foster home settings are from tourists or residents who find our website through a Google search. It is hard to avoid helping, but I would suggest not removing an animal from their setting to a hotel room or Airbnb, and then leaving and putting it back on the street. The cat can get disoriented and perhaps be in danger.

We truly hope to have more controlled community care for our strays in the future.
